about: The words of the cards of Northumbria and the Irish Sea (Data/encounters/northumbria_irish_sea_793.json), written 7 Oct 2026 by the region's weaver: a draft for the user to overwrite. Keys: northumbria_irish_sea.<port>.<card>.<slot>; do_<key> is an option's label, out_<key> what comes of it; art.<card id> says what the card's picture shows; northumbria_irish_sea.news.<name> is a news item a card posts.

entries.text: A Frisian hull
You have hardly a rope ashore before a tall man in a dark red cloak comes down the planks over the mud. He looks at the boat's lines before he looks at you.

Noon on a brown tidal strand under a grey Roman wall: a small clinker boat aground among mooring posts, and a tall bearded thegn in a dark red cloak with a silver ring pin standing on the planks above her, one hand on a worn sword hilt, looking down at the merchant in the boat; porters have stopped behind him to watch.
Built in the Danes' fashion and sailed in the Frisian. I know the cut of that cloak. Whose boat is she, and whose men are these?
The boat that is out of Dorestat and belongs to nobody. I asked a plain thing last time. I am asking it again.
You gave me a clever answer on this mud. I had it unpicked by evening. Do not do that twice.
The house I know now, and the boat. My brother Ecgric lay on this strand, about where your stern is. Unload. Sell through the host and through no one else.
There is a man at your steering oar who keeps his hood up in fair weather. Tell him I can count twenty years as well as he can.
The price is named and written. I come down to see whether your hold is full of wine or of silver. I can wait for either.
Say whose she is, and who sails in her
Say she is out of Dorestat, and no more
Ask him what would end it
Unload under his eye and say nothing

He hears the house's name, and the widow's, without moving. Then he nods once, as a man does who has been told the state of the tide. You may trade here through an English host, he says, and through nobody else.
He looks at you for a long breath and goes back up the planks. You have told him nothing, and he has noticed how carefully.
He asks a porter, who asks a boy, who knows whose casks these are. By evening he has the house's name, and yours beside it as the man who would not say it.
A number, he says, said before the archbishop, and silver on a cloak before my kin. He says it at once. He has had the answer ready for twenty years, and nobody has asked.
He stands on the planks until the last bale is up, and counts them. It is not his office to count them.
The host's bench
Wulfheard sits under his eaves, where he can see the whole lane down to the strand. He has a tally stick in one hand and has already cut a notch in it for you.

A long thatched house end-on to a muddy lane, a fenced yard with a storehouse on posts and a pig behind the fence: a broad fair-haired host of forty-five sits on the bench under the eaves with a horn cup and a bunch of notched sticks, beckoning the merchant in; late afternoon, the strand and tilted boats beyond.
A stranger with nobody to answer for him is a thief until the reeve is tired. Sit down. Now I answer for you, and you owe me three nights and all your news.
Your peg is where it was and nobody has hung a hat on it. Sit. Wool first, then wine, then whatever you are not telling me.
Bread is a third bark this year. If there is grain in that boat, sell it by daylight, and where the minster's almoner can see your face.
Ecgwulf has had your name out of you. Then you had better have the rest out of me. It is an old story and I was standing in it.
That stick with the black notch is Radger's. Four casks. I sold them the winter he ran and put the silver in a pot. I have never known whom to give it to.
It is paid. I saw it counted. Come in: there is a pot under my hearthstone that has waited twenty years for this evening.
Frisians on my bench again, and nobody watching the door. My father would have charged them double for the pleasure.
Lodge three nights under his roof (4 d)
Hear the year the Frisians ran, from a man who saw it
Take Radger's kept silver for the widow's house
Sit on the bench and give him your news
Three nights by his fire, with barley broth and every rumour of the strand. On the third morning he cuts your notch deeper: in law you are his man now, and he answers for what you do.

He was twenty-five. The men were mustering for a war, there was drink, a Frisian merchant, a count's son and a knife. Thirty hulls went down the river on one tide, and a ship's boy was pulled aboard the last of them by his hair. The dead youth's brother has come down to the strand ever since.

He lifts the hearthstone and counts out a pound of old pennies, black with soot: four casks, sold in the winter of the running. Then he breaks the stick with the black notch across his knee and puts both halves on the fire.
He asks three questions before he answers one, and by the time the cup is empty he knows what Dorestat pays for wool. You know what the minster's cellarer will give for wine. It is a fair exchange.
The price is named
In the porch of Saint Peter's the archbishop sits on a folding stool with a clerk at his elbow. Ecgwulf stands on one side with four of his kin. The other side is yours, and you are alone on it.

The stone porch of a minster in grey light: an archbishop in a dark vestment on a folding stool, a clerk with a wax tablet beside him; on the left a tall thegn in a red cloak with four armed kinsmen, on the right one Frisian merchant in a short cloak; between them an empty patch of flagstones.
A blood-price, before the Church. Good. Twenty years it has walked about this city like a dog nobody owns. Name your dead, thegn, and name your number.
Ecgric, Ecgwine's son, killed on the strand in the year of the muster by Radger of Dorestat. Three pounds of silver by weight. I will not be beaten down like a wool-seller.
There is a letter here from a scribe of Bede's house, who was a boy on the bank that day. He writes that the Frisian did not draw first. That does not unkill a man. It may shorten the sum.
My cousin's widow on the holy island sends word that this man has carried for the boys who were taken. She does not send word for nothing. I have heard her.
The Church stands witness and takes nothing. The clerk takes a penny for the wax. That is not the same thing.
Stand and hear the price named: three pounds
Ask that the scribe's letter be weighed in the sum
Say you cannot stand for another man's house, and go

The clerk writes it on wax and then on skin: seven hundred and twenty pennies by weight, to be counted on a cloak on the strand before the kin and two men who can count. Ecgwulf says his brother's name once more and goes out past you without touching his sword.

The archbishop reads it twice and looks at Ecgwulf over the top of it. A man who did not strike first is no murderer, he says, only a fool with a knife. Two pounds. Ecgwulf is silent for a long time. Then he says: two pounds, and the letter read aloud on the day.
Nobody stops you. The clerk rubs the wax smooth with his thumb. On the strand that afternoon the porters carry your bales as if they were somebody else's.
Silver on a cloak
The kin stand in a half circle on the strand at low water. A dark red cloak lies spread on the planks, and the archbishop's man has brought two who can count.

Low water on the muddy strand, grey morning: a half circle of ten English men and women in good cloaks, a dark red cloak spread on the planking with a small heap of silver pennies on it, a tonsured clerk and a broad host kneeling to count, the Frisian merchant standing opposite a tall thegn; the fortress wall behind.
There is the cloak. It was his. Put on it what was named, and I will say his name, and then your people may walk this mud like any others.
Two pounds, and the scribe's letter first. I gave my word in the porch. I do not like it and I will keep it.
Or half in silver, and for the rest the errand I named on the rock: wine for my lord's board through the lean season, carried at your own risk.
I have counted on this strand for thirty years. I shall count this slowly. Nobody is to say afterwards that it was done in a hurry.
Count out three pounds (720 d)
Count out the two pounds the letter left (480 d)
Pay half, and take his errand for the rest (360 d)
Say the silver is not yet gathered

Wulfheard counts it by twelves and the clerk says each pound aloud. Ecgwulf says: Ecgric. Then he folds the cloak over the silver and gives it to a woman of his kin. The next morning your steersman walks the whole length of the strand under his own name, slowly, and the host walks beside him.

The clerk reads the scribe's letter to the half circle first: a boy on the bank, a brawl, who drew. Then the silver is counted by twelves. Ecgwulf says his brother's name and folds the cloak. He does not look at the letter again, but he lets the clerk keep it.

Half is counted on the cloak. For the other half he takes your word before the clerk: six casks of Rhine wine to his lord's board within the year, at your own risk. Ecgric's name is said. It is finished when the wine is drunk, he says, and not before; but your people may walk the mud.
He picks the cloak up himself and shakes the sand out of it. It has waited twenty years, he says. It can wait for your next cargo. Not for the one after.
A third bark

Word that there is grain in your boat is up the lane before you are. A dealer is at your elbow with his purse open. At the back of the crowd a monk of the minster stands with his hands in his sleeves, listening for what you ask.

A lane of timber houses in a hungry year: thin townspeople pressed round a Frisian merchant and two open grain sacks on a trestle, a sleek corn dealer holding out a purse, and behind the crowd a quiet monk with his hands in his sleeves watching the merchant's face; flat grey light.
Whatever you ask, I give it, for the whole boat, now. You need not stand in this lane all day being looked at. Name it.
Wheat! There has been no wheat on this strand since Candlemas. A man could ask three times its worth and be thanked for it.
The minster buys nothing today. I am only here to hear a number. Take your time over it.
It rained blood on our roof in Lent, and then the heathen came to Saint Cuthbert's. People say the third thing will be hunger. They are a little late. It is here.
Cry a fair price, and sell by the sack to all comers
Ask what the famine will bear
Carry one sack of wheat up to the minster door first

You name a price a little over a common year's and sell by the sack to whoever stands in the line. It takes the whole day. The dealer goes away. The monk stays to the last sack, and then says only that the minster knows your boat now.
The dealer does not blink at the number. Nobody in the lane says a word against it either. They only look, and then go home. The monk has gone before the purse is shut.
The almoner takes it on his own shoulder and does not thank you until it is inside. Then he tells you what each dealer in the wic is paying, and which of them gives short measure.
The letter read aloud
The minster is full to the door. A priest stands by Saint Paul's altar with a letter from over the sea and reads it out a sentence at a time, first in Latin and then in English.

Inside a stone minster with small coloured windows: townspeople and a few armed king's men standing on a cold floor, a priest by an altar holding a letter up to the light and reading; on the north wall a dark stain runs down from under the lead roof.
'Never before has such a terror appeared in Britain as we have now suffered from a heathen people, nor was it thought that such a voyage could be made.' So writes Master Alcuin, to the king.
You are looking at the wall. In Lent it ran red from the north side of the roof, on a clear day. A slater says rust. The slater was not asked.
The chest by the door is for the boys the heathen carried off. Eleven pounds so far, and nobody yet who knows where to carry it.
On a feast the king's men must come to church. So on a feast we read the letter. They stand at the back. They hear it very well from there.
Stay and hear it to the end
Put silver in the chest for the boys (12 d)
Ask what is known of the boys

It is a long letter and a hard one: fine clothes, trimmed beards, feasting while the poor go cold. People weep. The king's men look at the floor. Afterwards the priest lets you have a fair copy to carry, since letters are written to travel.
A shilling of pennies goes in among the rest. The priest writes nothing down. He says God keeps that tally, and that he himself would only lose the stick.

Their names are with a monk called Sigewine, he says, who carries the master's letters and is to be found wherever there are books. Try the school. If he is not there, wait: he will be back for his cloak.
Saint Peter's day
It is the feast of the minster's own saint. The lane is swept, every board in the wic is bare, and a bell is ringing inside the old wall. The reeve leans on your trestle to make sure it stays bare.

A swept lane of timber houses on a bright midsummer morning: bare trestles, townspeople in their best walking up toward a grey Roman wall with a lead church roof behind it; a lean reeve with a staff resting one hand on the merchant's empty board; a cart of wool sacks waiting in the shade.
Saint Peter keeps the keys today, and I keep the strand for him. Nothing is opened till the Mass is sung. After it, sell what you like, and I take the king's share as on any day.
That cart is the minster's own clip, the first of the year. It goes when the bell stops, at the cellarer's price, to whoever is standing nearest. I did not tell you where to stand.
You were the one with the open board on the apostle's morning. I remember a face that has cost me an argument.
Go up to the Mass with your crew
Wait by the cart and buy the minster's wool (24 d)
Open your boards while the town is in church

The church is cold and full, and the glass throws red and blue on the heads in front of you. Your men stand quietly at the back among the carters. When you come down again the lane smells of roast meat and nobody is in a hurry.

The bell stops. The cellarer's boy names six pennies the sack, you say four sacks before he has finished the word, and it is done before the first townsman is through the gate. The reeve looks at the sky.
A few who love a bargain more than a sermon come back down the lane. You take twenty pennies before the reeve turns round, and have the cloth over the board again when he does.
The reeve does not shout. He lays his staff across your board and names the fine for trading on the apostle's feast, and a boy runs to tell the minster who paid it.
The satchel
A tall stooping monk is waiting by the door of the book room with a letter case under one arm and a sealed satchel he does not put down. He has been asking the scribes which Frisian has the dry boat.

The doorway of a school room lined with book chests: a tall, stooping, tonsured monk in a patched black cowl clutching a leather letter case and a wax-sealed satchel, speaking earnestly to the merchant; boys on a bench behind him pretending not to listen; cold window light.
Forgive me. You are the Frisian with the small boat? I need a passage, a dry corner for this satchel, and a day on which you will truly sail.
You again, thank God, and afloat. I have three letters and a psalter. The psalter does not swim. Neither do I.
I have not forgotten the last crossing. Nor, I think, has your bailing scoop. I ask again all the same.
I have the names of the boys who were taken from the island, and what the minster has gathered for them. What I have not got is anybody who goes north of the Tyne and comes back.
The ink has frozen in the horn twice this week. I mention it only because nobody else here will listen any longer.
Carry him up the coast to the holy island
Carry him over the sea to Dorestat
Take the names, and his letter for the priest at Dorestat
Say you sail when the wind says, not when a monk does

He is sick before the river mouth and apologises to each of your men in turn. Between bouts he tells you the boys' names from the bishop's own list, and what the minster will pay for any one of them alive.

He lies in the bottom of the boat on the satchel for most of the crossing. When the water is flat he sits up and makes your lookout read aloud to him, and corrects you both. You know the boys' names by heart before the Rhine mouth.
He says the names over twice so that you have them, and seals the letter in front of you with a borrowed candle. This to the priest on the dam, he says. If you die at sea, I shall be very put out.
He bows, apologises for having asked, and goes to ask the next boat, who will also refuse. He has been doing this for ten years and the letters still arrive.
A line about merchants

Torhthelm has a letter flat under his left hand and is copying from it with his right. When he sees a merchant in the doorway he stops, which he does for few people, and turns the leaf toward the light.

A cold room of slanted desks and book chests: a short, narrow-shouldered scribe with an ink-black thumb holds a letter toward a small window and points at one line with his penknife; the Frisian merchant leans in beside him; a boy rules lines at the next desk.
You trade over the sea. Then here is a thing about you in a book. Master Alcuin, to a friend in Ireland, some winters back. Stand out of my light.
'A quarrel has lately risen between King Charles and King Offa, so that on both sides the passage of ships is forbidden to merchants.' His pen shook at 'merchants'. Or it was a bad pen.
He does not say whether our ships are meant, or only the Mercians'. Scholars never write down the one thing a shipman needs.
You carry my copy of that line? Then it has travelled further than I ever shall. Tell me where it has been.
Ask what it means for a Frisian with English goods aboard
Pay him to copy the line fair (6 d)
Tell him what the quarrel has done to the price of wine

He thinks about it as he would about a hard place in a psalm. The kings forbade each other's merchants, he says at last. You are King Charles's man, so in King Offa's ports you are forbidden: but a toll man reads the hull and not the letter. He would not care to be your hull.

He writes it on an offcut of skin in a hand like a row of small black teeth, Latin above and English below, and dries it with sand. One sentence. In the right place, he says, one sentence is a charter.

He has no interest in wine and says so, and then fetches the cellarer, who has plenty. Three casks of Rhine wine for the altar and the high table before the year turns, at well over the strand's price, since so few ships come.
The moneyers' bench
The lean-to rings like a small bell. The moneyer lets the hammer fall once more, drops the coin in the bowl, and holds out his hand for your purse without being asked.

A lean-to against a stone wall: an oak block set in the earth floor with an iron die standing in it, a moneyer in a scorched apron holding the upper die and a short hammer, a boy laying a blank; in front a scale no bigger than a hand, and the merchant's open purse on the bench; charcoal glow behind.
Frankish pennies. Broad, pale, your king's name tied in a knot. Very pretty. They do not pass on this strand. Here it is our coin or it is the scale.
The Frisian purse. Put it down. I remember your silver: it rang well and you argued badly.
I will tell you a thing against my own trade. Our pennies stop at the Humber. Carry home wool, hides, jet. Do not carry home me.
They say your king has made his penny heavier. Then yours is worth more of mine than it was. I shall find a way to disagree.
You see what I strike now. Brass, tin and a memory of silver, by the thousand. I cut a handsome die for it. It deserves that much.
Change sixty pennies' weight for the strand's coin
Have him try a doubtful coin from your purse
Ask what a bucket of the small coin is truly worth
He weighs yours, counts out his, and keeps a tenth for the king and the fire. With the king's coin in your purse the reeve's man takes his share on the strand without the long argument about weights.
He drops it on the stone, listens, nicks it and hands it back. Good silver, badly struck. That is the right way round, he says, and most of the world manages the other.

He looks to see who is listening. Scrap, he says. A bronze-smith over the sea would give more for the bucket than any man here gives for what is in it. If a buyer offers you the king's coin by the bucket, admire it, and take fleeces.
The king has heard
A king's man finds you on the strand and walks you up to the hall without saying why. Inside, the benches are full, and the talk stops as you come through the porch.

A long timber hall with a hearth down the middle and full benches: a young king in a red cloak on the high seat leaning forward, thegns turned to stare, dogs under the boards; the Frisian merchant standing alone on the rushes just inside the carved door; firelight and smoke.
This is the Frisian who sold corn in my city at a price a poor man could say aloud. Look at him. I have thegns who could not do as much.
This is the Frisian who sold corn in my city in a hungry year. I am told the price. I had it said to me twice, to be sure of it.
The king is not angry. The king would only like the measure looked at, and the tally, and the boat. I have the afternoon free.
Priests write me letters about my sins and the cut of my beard. Nobody writes me a letter about bread. So I notice the man who brings some.
Take the king's word on the strand
Ask instead for the hall's wine custom
Stay for the reeve's counting, and pay what he finds (40 d)
Bow, say nothing, and go out by the porch
He says it before the benches: this man's boat lies on the Foss strand in the king's own peace, and the reeve takes half his share of her for a year. It will hold as long as the king does.
The king laughs and looks at his steward. Four casks of Rhine wine before next harvest, at well over the strand's price, and the steward is to remember the boat.
The reeve finds a measure a thumb short and a tally a sack long, as reeves can. Forty pennies in good silver, and the matter is closed. The king has already gone back to his meat.
Nobody stops a man who bows. On the strand the reeve's man looks at your boat a little longer than he did before, or you think he does.
Talk at the well
At the well in the waste ground the buckets stand full and nobody is carrying them home. The women stop talking when you come up, look at your short cloak, and decide that a foreigner does not count.

Waste ground of nettles and broken Roman tile between a fortress wall and a river: five women with yokes and full buckets standing close round a plank-lined well, one speaking low with a hand raised, the rest listening; the Frisian merchant waiting his turn with an empty bucket; a heron in the wet beyond; early light.
The king is dead. Killed by his own men, up at Corbridge, a week before the Litany. A carter brought it down the north road with his horse half dead under him.
They have made Osbald king, the one who burned a man in his house. Remember the name if you like. I would not cut it on anything.
Osbald is out again. Twenty-seven days. They have fetched Eardwulf back and hallowed him at Saint Paul's altar. That is three kings since Easter.
The hall is buying nothing. A steward does not buy when he cannot tell whose steward he will be tomorrow.
Carry the word up the coast yourself
Hold your wine for whoever is hallowed next
Shrug: wells are always killing kings
You have it from the well, and the well had it from the carter. It is true, as it turns out, and yours is the first sail to carry it north of the Tyne.
A hall that is buying nothing today will be feasting a new king within the month, and new kings pour freely. You keep the casks under their cover and let the other boats sell cheap.
It was true. You learn so at the next port, from a man who heard it later than you did and believed it sooner.
The building bank
A hull stands on the stocks with half her strakes on, and a pitch pot smokes on three stones. The wright has left his adze in a plank and walked down the bank to knock on your boat with his knuckles.

A firm river bank downstream of a town: a half-planked hull on stocks with clamps along her strakes, split oak under a thatch, a smoking pitch pot; in front a broad wright in a leather apron bends to knock on the side of the merchant's small clinker boat, the merchant watching from the mud; afternoon.
Danish work. Light. Somebody has kept her well, and somebody else has patched her in a hurry. Which of them are you?
She still floats. I knocked on her while you were up at the host's. Third strake, steer-board side. Do not look at me so. I only knock.
I boil my own pitch and it is never enough. Tar from the pine countries is what a hull wants, and no ship brings it this far up a river.
Take his order for tar from over the sea
Have him go over her on the mud (8 d)
Ask what a boat like her would cost new on his bank
Three barrels of pine tar by this time next year, he says, and he will pay a third over what the strand gives. He cuts it on a stick, splits the stick, and keeps the half with the bark.
He spends the ebb under her with a mallet and a twist of tarred wool, and comes out grey to the ears. Two rivets and a seam. Your men sleep the better for it on the Humber.
A winter, he says, twenty oaks, and two pounds of silver, half of it down. He looks at your face and adds that a second-hand one comes cheaper, whenever the river gives one back.
The alehouse on the old yard
Three tongues are being spoken on the bench outside. Inside, a woman with red hands and a string of amber between her brooches looks at you once, pours, and holds the cup back until you have spoken.

A low wattle alehouse with a bush on a pole over the door: inside, a trestle, a tub of ale with a dipper, a tafl board scratched on a plank, a hammer and a cross hung on one nail by the hearth; a strong fair-haired woman in an apron-dress with two bronze brooches holding a cup just out of the merchant's reach; evening firelight.
Sit. The first cup is paid for, like the rest. You have the sound of the Rhine mouth. Say 'eleven casks' for me. Yes. Rhine mouth.
I know you. You sat there, drank three and paid for four by mistake. I kept the difference for you. Here.
Wait. There is a stick in my roof older than the Danes in this town, with a Frisian house's notch on it, three nights deep. Show me your mark.
The house of the old stick. Your bench is the one by the hearth. It has been yours longer than this town has had a king worth naming.
To sell here and in the English king's ports both, a man wants somebody to stand for him. The old archbishop will, once, for a man who brings wax and does not waste his morning.
There is a new king. Do not learn his name yet. I have stopped until they last a winter.
Show her the house's mark
Send two cakes of wax to the archbishop, with her word
Hire the settler's son she vouches for (10 d)
Drink, and listen to three tongues at once

She fetches the stick down out of the thatch, black with a hundred winters of smoke, and lays your tally against it. The notches meet. She says nothing for a moment, which is rare, and then pours without counting.

A boy goes up to the minster with your name and the wax. Next day an old man with a white band over a mended vestment looks at you for as long as a short prayer takes, and says he will stand for you on both sides of the line. Once. You are not to make a liar of him.

His father came with the army and got a furrow. The son has looked at the furrow for eighteen years. He takes your ten pennies, gives eight to Thorgerd to keep for his mother, and is in the boat before you are.

A Dublin skipper is cheating a Lincoln man in bad English, and a monk is cheating them both in worse Danish. By the second cup you can follow all three. By the third you have agreed to nothing, which is a good evening.
The sky and the skull

In the kings' hall a heavy man in a blue cloak stands by the hearth with a horn in his left hand. He has been watching you find a place on the low bench, and seems to think you have chosen too humbly, or too soon.

A hall with beast-headed gable beams and a row of round shields along the wall: a heavy, grey-streaked poet in a king's blue cloak standing by the long hearth, drinking horn in his left hand, pointing the merchant from the low bench toward a higher one; men at dice by the door; smoky firelight.
A merchant in a king's hall. Sit low and listen. Or sit higher, if you can tell me one thing: in the earliest time, whence came the earth, and the sky over it?
You are still carrying my question about with you. It is heavy for its size. Most men put it down before Lincoln.
You have the giant's bones in your face. Say it, then, and say it loud. The king likes an answer he can hear.
The next question is not mine. Dublin's poet has it, and thinks it the better half. Go and let him tell you so.
So the sea has asked you its question too. Then here is the one that grows out of it: how did he get children, that grim giant, who never knew a giantess?
I have praised the feeder of ravens, the breaker of rings and the reddener of the wolf's tooth. All one king. He owed me for three.
Buy the first question (10 d)
Say whose flesh the earth was made of
Take the question that grows out of the sea's
Sit low and listen
He weighs your ten pennies in his palm as if they were a ring, finds them light, and gives you the question anyway, cut on a stick: whence the earth, whence the sky. The answer, he says, is a death.

You say it across the fire, and the dice stop. The poet gives the stanza back to you whole, bones and blood and the frost-cold skull, and the king has you moved up the bench to where the ale arrives sooner.

He does not sell this one. He says a man who has got so far down the giant's line is owed the next step, as a guest is owed fire. The last step of all, he says, is kept on the monks' island in the west, by a man who goes there to see his dead.
He names the king three ways before he names him plainly, and enjoys the wait. You understand one word in three and the price of nothing. It is still better than the rain.
Jet on the board

On a board at the street end of a narrow plot lie amber and jet, half cut: rings, pins, dice, a small cross. The man behind it puts down his saw and holds out a hand, palm up, for whatever is in your sack.

A street of narrow wattle plots, black and soft underfoot: a craftsman at a board strewn with half-cut jet rings, amber beads and a small jet cross, a bow-saw laid down, one hand held out palm up to the merchant, who is opening a sack of rough black stones; a pole lathe turning next door.
Raw stone? Put it here. No: do not tell me it is jet. Every man who ever sold me cliff told me first that it was jet.
The Frisian with the black sack. Tip it out. I shall find the shale in it by myself, as I did the last time.
You rubbed it on your sleeve before you handed it over. Good. Then you have been under the cliff, and somebody's grandmother has taught you.
Rings, pins, dice, small crosses. The Dublin men want it for arm rings. I do not ask why a man wants a black ring.
Sell him a sack of tested stone
Sell him a sack as it comes
Take his order for the season's best
Watch him cut a ring

He tries three lumps with a straw and a fourth on the fire, and then stops trying. Thirty-eight pennies by weight, with no talk. He says a man who sells him no cliff may come to his board before the others do.
He sorts it with his thumb. Most of it is true. Twenty-six pennies, and he tells you that you were lucky in your cliff.
He sorts it with his thumb into two heaps, and the larger heap is heavy and dull. Twelve pennies for the small one. The rest, he says, you may give to somebody you dislike.

Three sacks before next midsummer, he says, picked after the winter falls and tried by the straw, and he will pay well over the common weight. He gives you a bad ring to show the gatherers what he does not want.

He saws a flat round, bores it, and works it on a spindle with sand and then with his thumb until it takes the light like wet coal. It is a morning's work, he says, for a thing a Dublin man will lose at dice by evening.
The leaf that asks who drives it
The book chest stands with its lid split, and a thin monk with a healing cut through his lip is sorting loose leaves into piles on the floor. He looks at your feet before he looks at you.

A plain timber writing room with the shutters wide: a split book chest, loose leaves in careful piles on the floor, one leaf with a boot print across a line of verse; a narrow, pale monk with a cut lip kneeling among them, one hand raised to stop the merchant in the doorway; a calfskin drying on a frame; clear sea light.
Mind the floor. Each of those piles is a book, or was one. You are standing on the Psalms. Thank you.
The merchant. I have a list for you. It is shorter than the last one, because I have given up hoping for the blue.
One quire of English verse went three ways when they turned this room out. I have a leaf of it: the storm that walks the land. Ten pennies for a fair copy. I grudge every one.
Two more leaves went astray. The wind had them, or somebody's shirt did. I have my own opinion which.
That fold. That boot mark. Where did you... No. Do not tell me yet. Put it down flat.
Torhtred kept it flat. Tell him I said so. Tell him nothing else that I said.
Buy a fair copy of the leaf (10 d)
Give him the leaf you carried from Gyrwe
Ask him what a book is worth
Step carefully and leave him to his piles

He writes it out in a hand you could cut yourself on: who sends me on my journey, when I rise up strong, and burn the halls, and shake the woods? He will not give the answer. He says the other two leaves would.

He looks at the leaf, then at the fold in it, and says a short word in Latin that is not in the psalter. Then he asks how Torhtred's hands are in the cold. A cake of the house's wax is yours, he says, and anything in your chest copied here for nothing.

He reckons it aloud: so many calves, a scribe's year, the gold. Then what a king's church would give for it, and what the metal weighs on a heathen's scale. The two sums are very far apart. A merchant, he says, lives in the gap.
You go out backwards. He has already forgotten you and is holding two leaves to the light to see whether their ruling matches. It does not. He sighs like a man putting down a heavy sack.
The half door

A thatched store with a half door, and a beam scale hanging in the opening. A stout monk with a ring of red hair round a sunburned crown has his elbows on the door and has been counting your casks since you rounded the point.

A thatched storehouse with a half door and a beam scale hung in the opening: a stout, red-haired, sunburned monk leaning on the door with a tally stick and iron keys, grinning at the merchant; behind him in the dark, casks on their sides and wax cakes under a cloth; a boy sweeping up spilled corn.
A keel with casks in her. Come to the half door, friend. I tell you now: we pay badly and pray well.
There you are. I told the brothers you would come back, and they said merchants never do. I had a loaf on it.
You promised me wax, and here you are. So you have the wax or you have a good story. I will take the wax.
Our own farm at Norham sent excuses in place of corn. The reeve there says famine. His horse is fat.
They drank the altar wine on the beach and left the cask. A good cask. I use it. I do not tell the bishop which one it is.
You saw a man by my fire in the year of three kings, and said nothing to anyone. I noticed. I notice silence. I get so little of it.
You have been to the mother house and carry the old abbot's word. Then this cup is from the bishop's own jar. And I have a message for a guest-master I have never set eyes on.
Promise him wax before next Easter
Leave a cake of wax at the half door, as a gift
Leave two sacks of barley for the brethren
Put your goods on his scale and take what the house gives

Three cakes, he says, by Candlemas if God is kind and by Easter if he is only fair, at a third over the common price: paid in wool, in thanks and in what silver is left. He cuts it on a stick and kisses the stick.
He weighs it in his two hands before he will believe it. There is a bed nearest the fire in the guest house, he says, that is kept for the letter carrier. From tonight it is kept for you as well.
He counts the sacks twice, though there are two. Bread corn this year, he says, is the same as a relic, only more use. A boy sweeps up what spills, grain by grain.
He says what a thing weighs before he says what it is, and what the house can give before you ask. It is not much. It is exactly what he said, to the grain.
The broken cross

A woman in a dark blue gown stands by the bishop's cross, whose head lies in the grass beside it in pieces. She has been waiting for you to finish at the cellarer's door, and does not pretend otherwise.

A graveyard of low mounds scattered with white pebbles, feet to the sea: a tall stone cross with its carved head lying broken in the grass, and beside it an upright woman past forty in a dark blue gown and a linen head-cloth with a thread of gold, hands folded, facing the merchant; fresh square-cut graves at the near end; wind.
You are the Frisian's boat. You will be asked for nothing in my house but news. Which ports do you make this year, and how far north?
Welcome back. I looked for your sail at each feast. Tell me first whether you have been north. Then eat.
You have the bishop's list. My sister's son Wigfrith is the third name on it. Three families have sold cattle, and nobody knows yet whom to pay.
They tell me Ecgwulf has your boat's name at York. He is my husband's cousin. He listens to me about one time in three, which is more than he listens to bishops.
I have sent to York. I said what I know of you and nothing that I do not. If he asks more of you than is just, tell me, and I shall be sorry I wrote.
My husband's brother stood on the rock and watched the smoke. He says they had no ships ready. They had horses.
Promise to tell her first, at her own door, whatever is found
Ask her to speak for you to her husband's kin at York
Add silver to what the three families have raised (20 d)
Give her the news of the coast, and ask nothing

She nods as if a price had been agreed. If the boy is dead, she says, you will tell me straight, at this door, before you tell the bishop. He will grieve in Latin. I should like to do it first in English.

She has known the story for twenty years and tells it shorter than any man: a muster, drink, a knife, and a boy dead who was the better of two brothers. She will send word that you have carried for the island. What Ecgwulf does with the word, she says, is Ecgwulf's.

She counts it into a linen bag that already holds very little, and writes nothing down. She will remember it, she says, to the penny, and so will three households on the mainland who do not know your name yet.

She asks a hard question as if it were about the weather, and listens to the whole answer. When you have done she sends a girl for bread and a bowl. A friend is good far or near, she says, and better near; mine are far, so I feed merchants.
The rock in the fast

It is a fast day. There is a thread of smoke on the black rock off the shore, where one of the brothers keeps it alone, and in the guest house the pot holds barley and nothing else. Your men have noticed.

A hump of black rock a bowshot off a shingle shore at half ebb, turf on its top, a low wall of piled stones and a thin thread of smoke; eider ducks on the water round it; on the shore a stout monk holding a water skin out to the merchant and pointing over the weed and pools; cold spring light.
No meat today, friend, and none for the house until the feast. The broth is honest. I do not say it is good.
One of ours is out on the saint's rock with a sack of barley and a psalter. At the ebb somebody carries his water over. Today it is my knees' turn, and my knees decline.
The saint's own day falls in the fast. So we keep his feast on barley. He would have thought it too much.
You carried the water. The saint had otters to dry his feet. I have a Frisian. We take what we are sent.
Keep the fast with the house, crew and all
Let the men eat their salt pork aboard, out of sight
Carry the brother's water out over the weed at the ebb

Your men eat barley and look at you. The brethren notice, and say nothing, which here is praise. By evening one of your crew has asked how the saint stood all night in the sea, and has been told at length.
The boat lies behind the shingle bank and the wind is off the land. Nobody ashore smells anything. Your men are cheerful and a little ashamed, in that order.
The wind goes round. The smell of frying pork walks up the beach and in at the guest-house door. At supper the cellarer says nothing at all, in a very marked manner.

It is further than it looks, and the weed is like wet eels. The brother on the rock takes the skin without a word, since he is keeping silence, and blesses the boat with two fingers. Your men, who watched from the shingle, are easier in their minds than a blessing ought to make them.
The boatman's pole
A short, wide man with a face like a dried apple is standing on the shingle with a sounding pole taller than himself, looking at where you have put your boat. He has been looking for some time.

A shelving shingle beach inside the sands, black weed along the tide line, two small tarred boats drawn up: a short, wide, weathered boatman in a sealskin jerkin, bare-legged, leaning on a tall sounding pole and pointing with his chin at the merchant's boat; behind, a ridge of black rock and a lead church roof catching the light; terns.
You came in on the last of the flood. Lucky, or taught? Pull her up past the weed line. She comes higher than you think.
Same boat, same place on the shingle. You listen. Most do not, and I get their anchors.
Long ships, low, more oars than I could count. They went north with the land close on the left hand. Men who knew this coast, or had one aboard who did.
I got two brothers out by the hair. The third had his habit on, and wet wool is an anchor.
You have the look of a man with a question he was told not to ask. Ask it. I can always not answer.
I told you which rock. I did not tell you the way in. That is the man under the kings' rock, and he will want his reason in writing.
Ask what rock holds its breath under the north-east wind
Hire him to take you out by the south (2 d)
Help him haul the house's boat above the weed line

He looks at you for a long time. Then he points with his pole at the Farne rocks, low and grey in the south-east, and says which one, and that there is a gut behind it with deep water at any tide. He has never taken a boat in. Bacga under the kings' rock has, and tells nobody.

He stands in your bow with the pole and says four words between the beach and deep water. All four are about the tide, whom he calls she. Your steersman says afterwards that it was the best lesson he ever had from a man who would not look at him.

It takes six of you, and the cellarer's opinion. When she is chocked he looks at the knot your man has tied, unties it, and ties it again the same way. It will do, he says. From him, the cellarer tells you later, that is a feast-day sermon.
The board by the fire

By the guest-house fire a game stands half played: pieces of bone round one of blue glass with a white crown. A well-dressed man sits behind it alone. The brethren will sit down with him, he says, but they will not stake.

A long hut with a fire down the middle and benches along the walls: a board scored in squares with bone pieces set round one of blue glass with a white crown; a well-dressed thegn with a ring pin sitting behind it, chin on fist, waving the merchant to the stool opposite; two pilgrims with their feet in a tub; smoke and firelight.
You play? Good. These holy men will move a piece for charity and never for a penny. I have been winning nothing off them for three days.
The Frisian who took my penny. Sit. I have thought about that corner for a month.
Or take a question for the road. What beast is that, all girdled with iron, which kills the flocks? It has eight horns, and no head.
Your bed is the one nearest the fire. The letter carrier has the other side of it when he comes. He talks in his sleep, in Latin.
Play him for a penny a game
Take his question away with you
Tell him what stands on the board with eight horns
Eat the broth and sleep
You lose the first game, learn his opening, and take the next three. He pays without a word and sets the pieces up again before you can stand.
He has had three days to practise on monks who would not stake. He takes three pennies off you between the broth and the bell, and is the happiest man on the island.

He says it over once more so that you have it right: girdled with iron, killing the flocks, eight horns and no head. He had it from a Northman in his father's hall, he says, who would never tell him the answer either.

You touch the blue glass piece in the middle of his board. He stares at it, and then begins to laugh, and has to explain to two pilgrims and the cellarer what he is laughing at. He pays you six pennies for it. He has owed that answer, he says, since he was a boy.
Barley, a little fish, and a fire that somebody else keeps in all night. The thegn sets his pieces out again alone, and is still looking at them when you close your eyes.
A guest who cannot stay

A quiet man sits by the cellarer's fire with the mark of a sword belt worn into his tunic, and no sword. The cellarer says only that the house has a guest who cannot stay. Down on the shingle the boatman is looking at your boat, and then at the tide.

Dusk on a shingle beach inside the sands: a tarred monastery boat being made ready by three monks, and beside it the merchant's small clinker boat; a weathered boatman with a tall pole between the two, and on the bank above a cloaked, unarmed man of rank looking down at both; a lead-roofed church behind against a yellow sky.
He goes north tonight, to the king of the Picts, in the house's boat, with three of the brothers. Yours is the better sea boat. I say what I see. The tide serves for an hour.
I was a king at Easter. I shall not tell you it was a good month. I have a ring worth more than your cargo, and I need to be somewhere else by morning.
A deacon over the sea once wrote to me that I should turn monk. I took it for an insult. It begins to look like advice.
You heard at York who he is, then. Good. It saves me from not telling you.
Take him north along the coast yourself
Stand aside, and keep your mouth shut
Cross to the rock and tell the new king's men where he is

Three nights north, close in, with the land on the left hand and a man in the bow who never once looks back. On a shingle beach under strange hills he pulls a ring of twisted gold and silver off his arm, the best part of a pound, and puts it in your hand. The new king's men will ask every skipper who lay at the island this month. You know that already.
The house's boat goes out on the top of the tide with four oars and a psalm. The cellarer brings you the end of a loaf and sits down beside you without a word, which from him is a long speech.

The gate-thegn hears you out and has thirty pennies counted to you from the steward's box, as a man pays a toll. By the time his men are over the sand the boat has gone. The bishop does not send for you. Nobody on the island sends for you again while he lives.
The bishop counts
Higbald stands in the open doorway of the church, where the hinges were, with a list in his hand. He counts what is in your face before he counts anything else.

A long low church sheathed in grey lead, its doorway standing open with the hinges torn out: in it a gaunt, white-tonsured bishop past sixty in a patched undyed habit, a plain wooden staff in one hand and a written leaf in the other, looking steadily at the merchant; daylight on a swept floor behind him.
You came in on the same beach they did. Forgive the brothers for watching you. What do you carry, and where do you go after this?
The boat I know. I have kept count since you left: nothing more is gone, and nothing has come back.
The abbess of Hild's house asks whether I have moved the saint. She asks it plainly. I shall answer in the same way.
That is a tally. I know what is counted on it without being told. Give it here. Carefully. It is the first thing anyone has brought me that points anywhere.
I have the list written twice. One is for a king who may pay. The other is for the mother house in the west, which will do the only thing that has always worked.
A man asked a night's shelter at the saint's body, and you sold the news of it for thirty pennies. I pray for you. I should like you to know that it is an effort.
Hear his answer for the abbess
Give him the rune-cut tally from the Tyne
Take the second list, for the mother house in the west
Ask his blessing on the boat

The saint chose his island and stays on it, he says. But a book can be written twice and a bone cannot. Let her copy what she has and send the copies where no ship comes. He has it written, three lines, and seals it with a borrowed ring, his own being among the things on the list.

He holds it as if it were hot. The scribe copies the owner's mark onto the list, beside the names. A cake of wax and a fleece come down to the boat that evening with no message, which is how this house says a thing it cannot afford to say.

It is a short leaf: the dead for the altar, the living for letters, the boys for both. He folds it into a piece of oiled skin himself. If you ever round the north and come to Columba's island, he says, give it into the abbot's own hand. If you do not, burn it. Do not sell it.

He comes down to the shingle to do it, which takes him some time, and says the prayer for those at sea with his hand on your stem. Then he counts your crew, from habit, and seems glad the number is the one he was told.
The cleft gate
Steps are cut up through a cleft in the black rock, worn as smooth as a bowl. At the top a lean man with a spear stands between you and a strip of sky, and asks his questions downhill.

A narrow cleft in a black rock with steps cut up through it: at the head of the stair, against a strip of sky and the gable of a timber hall, a lean fair-haired thegn in a grey cloak with a spear and a mended shield slung behind him, looking down at the merchant climbing; spears leaning in the shadow.
That is far enough. Name the boat, the port and the cargo, in that order. I count every sail now. I did not always.
The Frisian boat. Come up. Tell me what you met between here and the Tyne: sails, smoke, anything that floats.
Three sails, at the hour of terce, wind in the north-east. Forty men, no boats, and the tide over the flats. Nobody asks me. I say it anyway.
You have the bishop's list. Say the names. I knew one of the fathers. I taught his elder boy to throw a spear, and the boy went to sea with a Frisian.
You have my ring. I do not ask where it is. I ask whether it has bought anything yet.
They have cut the turf for a beacon on the west point, and two boats are promised. It is not a boy. But it is a thing that can be counted.
You bring it from York that the king is dead. A rider brought it the same night. It is still news to hear it from a man who is not afraid to say so.
The new king's reeve asks who carried Osbald north from the island. He asks every skipper. He has not asked me which boat sits lightest on that shingle, so I have not said.
Tell him what ships you met coming north
Say the boys' names to him
Tell him to keep his ring, and build a beacon and two boats
Bring him word that one of the boys lives
He has you say it twice: how many, how rigged, which way they lay. He cuts three notches on a stick already full of them. A sentry is paid to be afraid, he says. I am learning my trade late.

He hears the names out, looking over your head at the island. Then he takes off his silver arm-ring, a mark's weight, and puts it in your hand. Carry it north, he says, toward any one of them. He asks for no witness.

You say that a ring buys one boy if it buys any, and a fire on the west point warns the whole coast. He does not like it. He thinks about it with his jaw. Then he says a Frisian has just told a king's thegn his duty, and that he will see about the turf.

He says nothing for a while. Then he asks which one, and whether the boy still has his letters. After that the gate is yours: his wardens carry your bales up the steps, and he gives you the riddle he keeps for men he has begun to trust. I am a lone thing, he says, wounded with iron, and no leech heals me.
The dish under the dinner

The steward has a trestle in the gate-hall door with a balance on it, and he looks at your grain as a man looks at a fire in winter. Down in the vill an old woman in a checked shawl is looking at it too, and not asking.

The doorway of a timber gate hall on a rock: a stout, balding steward behind a trestle with a balance and a bundle of tally sticks, two open sacks of wheat before him; beyond and below, small in the green vill under the rock, an old woman in a checked shawl standing with her arms folded, looking up; grey hungry-year light.
Half as much again as it fetches at home, in picked fleeces and sound hides. The hall must eat. I do not say that is just. I say it is sixty mouths.
There are nine houses down there with nothing. I can name them. He can count them. Neither of us can feed them.
You will have been told about the saint and the dish. Everybody tells merchants about the dish. I am the steward. I am not paid to be a saint.
Sell the wheat to the hall for fleeces and hides
Measure it out in the vill, for what they can give
Sell half to the hall, and tithe the rest at the church door
Keep it under the cover for York
He weighs it in, counts the fleeces out and calls the price a good thought. The hall eats. On your way down through the vill nobody says anything, and a child is called indoors.

The priest measures it out at Aidan's church with the old scorched post at his back. They pay in eggs, a few dark pennies and one good knife. Your name is to be said there at Mass on Saint Aidan's day from now on, between the sick and the king.

Two sacks go up the steps and are paid for in fleeces. The rest is sold below at a fair price, less a tenth laid at the church door. The steward says it is not how he would have done it. The old woman says it is not how the saint did it either, and that it will do.
The steward watches the cover go back over the sacks and says that York is a thought, certainly. He does not say what kind.
A thought
There is no market on the rock. There is a trestle in a doorway, a balance, a bundle of notched sticks, and a stout mild man who calls every price a thought before he refuses it.

Inside the door of a long timber hall stacked with sacks, butter tubs and bundled hides: a stout, bald, mild-faced steward of fifty at a trestle with a small balance, counting on notched sticks, a wine cask stood on end before him; the merchant opposite with folded arms; wet-wool gloom and a shaft of light from the door.
A merchant. We have no market, so you are looking at it. What is in the boat? Do not say cloth.
You again. Good. Sit. I have kept the fleeces I spoke of, and thought of a new way to underpay you.
Sixty for the cask is a thought. Forty and two bundles of hides is a better thought. Think it with me.
Our pennies are little dark things. Take wool. Nobody at Dorestat will bite one of these and smile.
When a king changes, the first man through the gate asks for my keys and the second for my tallies. I give the keys gladly.
Take forty pennies and two bundles of hides for a cask
Hold out for picked fleeces, and nothing else
Promise him wine before Martinmas
Sit, and let him think aloud

The cask goes up to the high board on two wardens' shoulders. The pennies are small and dark, the hides are sound, and he has thrown in the string. He says it has been a pleasure to be robbed so politely.
He thinks about it through two more thoughts and a silence, and then has ten sacks of the rent wool brought out, the long white kind. He looks at them going down the steps as at ten friends.
He hears you out, says that it is a thought, and puts the cover back over his fleeces. The cask stays in your boat. The high board, he says, has drunk ale before.

Three casks before the household starts eating its rents, he says, and he will give a quarter over the common price in whatever you will take that is not silver. He will remember your name to whoever is king by then.

He tells you what the rock lacks this month, which vills paid short, and how much the last king's men ate. By the end you know the price of everything on this coast and have sold nothing. He seems to feel that is a fair morning.
Three sails again

At the well on the top of the rock the women have left their buckets and are all looking out to sea. Somebody has seen sails beyond the outer islands. Below, in the vill, they are already driving the sheep inland.

The bare top of a black rock with a square well mouth and a windlass: a knot of women with yokes and abandoned buckets all staring seaward past low grey islands, one pointing; a wiry fisherman in a sealskin cap beside them shrugging at the merchant; far below, sheep being driven inland from thatched houses; bright wind.
Three of them, low, out past the far rocks, the same as the last time. My man saw them. Well. His brother saw them, and told him.
The steward is selling the rent fleeces for whatever he can get, before they are taken for nothing. If you have silver, this is your morning.
I have looked. I see a sea, some rocks and a number of seals. But I am a liar about seals, as everybody knows, so nobody asks me.
Row out with Bacga and look for yourself
Buy the steward's fleeces at the frightened price (30 d)
Put to sea at once, southward, while there is water

Past the inner rocks, where the gate cannot see, there is one fat trader out of the Humber, reefed down, and a great many seals. It was not true. You carry that up the steps yourself, and the gate-thegn, who has forty men standing to arms, looks at you as at a man who has paid a debt of his.

Eight sacks for thirty pennies. By noon the sails have turned into a coaster and two fishing boats from the Tweed, and the steward has understood what he sold and to whom. He says it was a thought. He does not say it kindly.

You are over the bar on the half ebb with your men rowing like men with wolves behind them. There were no wolves. At the next port a skipper who lay under the rock that night asks, pleasantly, what you were running from.
Oswald's Mass
It is the harvest month and the week of Oswald's Mass. The small stone church on the top of the rock is full, and the priest stands at the north side of the altar with his hand on a cloth.

A small lime-washed stone church with narrow windows letting in bars of sea light: a thin, tonsured priest in a clean stole at the north side of the altar, lifting a cloth from a silver case in which a pale wrapped hand lies; household men and women from the vill crowded close, the merchant among them at the back; wax smoke.
A king sent his own dinner out to the poor at this gate, and the silver dish after it, broken small. His bishop took his hand and said: may it never grow old. Bede has it. I keep the key.
I lift the cloth. It is a hand. It has nails. I have looked at it these many years, and it has not learned to look old.
If you sail north and see an English boy with a shaved crown growing out, ask him his name. Only that. Then come and tell me.
Lay alms at the shrine (6 d)
Make a vow for the boat, with your hand on the altar rail
Stand at the back and watch the cloth lifted

Six pennies on the step, among the candle ends. The priest does not look at the coin. He looks at your men, who are looking at the hand, and says the saint was a great giver to seafarers, having been one in his exile.

You promise a candle the height of your steersman if the boat comes home whole before Martinmas. The priest writes it on a tablet, which is more than you expected. A vow made here, he says, has held a crew together through worse than weather.

It is small and pale and whole, and nobody in the church breathes while it is uncovered. Then the cloth is down, and a child asks loudly whether the king has his other hand with him in heaven, and is taken outside.
A grave in the sand

In a hollow of the sand hills south of the rock a grave is open, and a dead man lies beside it sewn into a cloak. He came off a hide boat from the west with a fever and no kin. An old woman in a checked shawl is short of bearers.

A hollow in sand hills out of the wind, low mounds in rows with here and there a stone set on edge, marram grass bending: an open grave, a long body sewn in a cloak beside it, a small upright old woman in a checked shawl with a ring brooch, a thin priest with a stole, and the merchant's four crewmen standing awkwardly with ropes; the black rock filling the sky behind.
He was from the western isles, by his speech, the little there was of it. Tall, with bad teeth. Half this field came here over water, as I did. He will have company.
I want four to lower him, and one who can say a word in a tongue he would know. The priest has the Latin. The Latin is for God. I want a word for him.
I bury her strangers, and she argues with me about Easter over the grave. It is the nearest thing either of us has to a feast.
If you ever go round to Columba's island, say that Muirenn of the rock keeps the true Easter in her heart and the Roman one in church. The old abbot will laugh. He knew my brother.
You carried my word west and brought his back. He remembered my brother's name. I shall be buried facing that way. See to it, if you are here.
Lend four of your men to lower him
Pay for the ale to be drunk over him (4 d)
Take her word for the abbot of Columba's island

Your men let him down on two ropes, feet to the east. One of them, who has an island grandmother, says the Our Father in a kind of Irish, badly. The old woman lays a white pebble on the sand and says it was well enough said for a man in a hurry.

She brews it herself, and takes your pennies only because they are foreign and bright. The vill drinks to a man none of them knew. By the third cup he has been a pilgrim, a king's son and a seal, and nobody can prove otherwise.

She makes you say it back twice: Muirenn of the rock, the true Easter in her heart and the Roman one in church. And a cheese goes with it, she says, which you are to hand over and not eat, however far it is.
The smiths' ward

One forge burns white, and a short, very broad man is twisting rods of iron together like a woman plaiting hair. He does not hear you come in. When he sees you he shouts, since that is the only way he can hear himself.

A low timber shed on a cobbled path: a white-hot forge, charcoal heaped under a lean-to, and a short, very broad smith with singed hair and a leather apron to the shins twisting glowing rods together with tongs; hammer-scale on the floor; the merchant in the doorway with a bundle of iron bars on his shoulder.
What? Speak to this ear. Iron? If it is Frankish bar I will look at it. If it is Frankish swords, get off my floor.
The boat man. That last bar welded sweet. Bring me the same and I will show you something twisted.
The blade that hangs in the hall is six rods. Six. I can do four, and four is more than York can.
The steward pays in promises. I have a shed full of them. They do not burn hot.
Your blade is in the fire or it is in my head. Either way it is not in your hand. Two winters, I said. Count them yourself.
Sell him two bundles of good bar iron
Ask him to make a blade for your house
Take his order for Frankish bar
Stand clear of the sparks and watch him weld

He rings each bar on the anvil, breaks one to see the grain, and pays half as much again as the strand would. Then he shouts a riddle at you over the bellows: a lord's shoulder-friend, bright, wire-wrapped, that takes no wife and is cursed by women. He will not say what hangs at your friend's hip.

He will take no silver down and name no day. A knife is three days and a spearhead a week, he says, but a blade with a pattern in it is two winters, and you are not to come asking. He spits in the quench trough, which here is a seal on the bargain.

Four bundles of the clean Rhine bar before the next hay harvest, and he will pay well over the common price, out of his own purse and not the steward's promises. He shows you a bad bar so that you will know one.

He twists four rods left and right and left, lays them together and brings them to a heat he judges by colour alone. When he strikes, the sparks go past your ear like bees. Good iron and a bad smith make a bad knife, he shouts. Bad iron and a good smith make a liar.
Two winters
The smith's boy comes down the steps to the strand to say that his father wants you now, before the light goes. In the shed a long thing lies on the anvil under a greased cloth.

Evening in a smith's shed, the forge burning low and red: a broad smith drawing a greased cloth off a long sword laid on the anvil, its blade showing a rippled pattern like water over sand in the firelight; a boy holding a lamp; the merchant leaning in.
Four rods, twisted left and right and left, and an edge welded on after. Hold it to the fire. See it run like water over sand? That is not painted on. That is the iron.
I do not sell this. A blade like this is given, or it is taken off a dead man. I give it. You brought iron that welded sweet, and never once told me to hurry.
Take the blade for your house
Ask him to give it to the thegn of the gate instead

It goes into a plain scabbard older than the blade, and from there into the bottom of your sea chest, wrapped in a fleece. It is a gift fit for any lord's hall on either side of the sea, or a thing for an heir to find and wonder how a Frisian came by it.

He stares at you with his good ear turned, to be sure. Then he carries it up to the gate himself, still in its cloth, and says only: from the Frisian, and stop brooding. From that day your boat is waved up the steps like the household's own.
The gut between the rocks

A wiry man in a sealskin cap is sitting on your gunwale when you come back down the steps, as if the boat were a bench put there for him. He has fish scales in his beard and an opinion about where you have moored.

A shallow tide inlet under a wall of black rock, boats tilted on wet sand: a wiry, wind-red fisherman in a sealskin cap and jerkin perched barefoot on the gunwale of the merchant's boat, gutting knife on a cord round his neck, grinning and pointing out to sea where low grey islands show; gulls and terns overhead.
That is a pretty boat to put on those rocks. A penny a day, and I will show you where the rocks are not.
Still afloat! I told my wife you would be. I told her otherwise as well, to be safe.
There is a gut out there with deep water at any tide. I am not saying where. Bring me a reason, in writing, since you are so clever.
Eadstan pointed with his pole, did he? He can point. Pointing is not a way in.
Nobody else, mind. Not your steersman's cousin. The saint's ducks nest on the way in, and they are particular about company.
Kill one of the saint's ducks and your nets come up empty for a year. My uncle tried it. He is a farmer now.
Read him the three answers of the storm leaves
Offer him silver for the secret (240 d)
Hire him to take you through the islands (1 d)
Let him talk about seals

He laughs, says that monks should mind their own rocks, and takes your boat out on the half ebb. Between two skerries that look like one there is a gut with a shingle bed and no swell, hidden from the gate and from the sea road. No toll man has ever stood there. He shows you the marks once.
He takes the pound, counts it twice, and shows you a landing among the inner rocks that will take a boat at high water and break her at low. It is a secret, he says. He never said it was the secret.

He steers with one bare foot on the oar and talks the whole way, mostly lies. But he puts you through the islands on a falling tide without once looking at the water, and names every rock as if it owed him money.

There are fifteen islands or twenty, he says, depending on who is counting and whether he is still dry. The seals are the size of oxen. One of them, he swears, is the size of the steward, and has the same look about the eyes.
The low end of the hall
The steward has found you a place at the low end of the hall for a feast. Half way up the bench sits a tall man from York in a dark red cloak, who has seen you and gives no sign of it.

A long hall with carved door-posts, shields over the benches and a hearth three men long, full of feasting men and dogs: at the low end by the door the Frisian merchant on the end of a bench with a horn cup; half way up, a tall thegn in a dark red cloak looking straight ahead; a flushed household man on his feet, arguing.
A deacon over the sea writes that our sins fetched the heathen. Our sins. I should like to see the deacon stand a watch on this wall in a north-easter.
They are angry at a letter. A man is only angry at a letter when it has come to the right house.
You sit at the low end and I sit here. That is as it should be until a number has been said. I do not eat with what my brother is owed.
The price is named. I am not a hard man. My lord's board has been dry since the hungry season began. There is a thing you could carry in place of half the silver.
Come up the bench. It is paid, and the hall knows it. Sit where a man sits who owes nothing.
Say what you heard read at York, when they ask the stranger
Ask him what the errand is
Keep your eyes on your cup

You give them the letter's own words, flatly, as a man reports a price. There is a silence, and then an old thegn says that at least the Frisian got it right. The talk turns to boats, and why the rock has none.
You get as far as the fine clothes and the trimmed beards. A household man asks whether merchants are now paid to carry sermons, and for the rest of the evening your cup is filled last.

Six casks of Rhine wine to his lord's board within a year of the day, carried at your own risk, in place of half the silver. He says it as a man reads out a boundary. He has thought of it for some time, and he would rather have the silver.

The meat is good and the ale is better than the steward's prices would suggest. Nobody asks the stranger anything. When you go out past the upper bench the tall man from York moves his feet out of your way, which is something.
A nephew home
You bring the young man up the steps yourself. In the gate hall a heavy man with keys at his belt looks at him for a long moment, the way a man looks at a field he had thought was his.

The door of a timber gate hall on the rock: a heavy grey-bearded reeve with a ring of keys staring at a thin young man in a worn Irish cloak who stands very straight; the merchant a pace behind the young man; a warden with a spear looking from one to the other; sea haze beyond.
Osgar. My brother's boy. We were told the rock on the Clyde fell, and every man in it was sold over the water. I had Masses said. They were not cheap.
His father died at York with the kings. The land is not large. I have held it since, and held it well. I do not say that to be thanked.
I can tally in two tongues and read a little. I kept a dealer's sticks for a winter. I should like to be asked what I want. It is some time since anybody did.
Ask only what he cost you, and leave him with his kin
Let Osgar say what he wants
Name a ransom fit for a reeve's heir

The uncle pays what the dealer was paid and half a pound over, in fleeces fairly priced and some hacked silver. A landing on this shore without a gift, he says, for as long as he keeps the keys. The young man walks to the well by himself and stands looking at the sea, of which he has had enough.

He says he would sooner keep a Frisian's tally than fight his uncle for nine hides of thin land. The uncle is relieved, and ashamed of being relieved, and sends down a cheese whenever your sail is seen after that. Toll men find it harder to cheat a boat with a clerk in her.

You name a pound. The uncle looks at the wardens, who are looking at him, and pays it rather than be seen to weigh his brother's son. He will know your boat again. He does not say that he will be glad to.

The uncle says a dealer's price is a dealer's price, and that he had already paid for the Masses. He gives you what you gave at Dublin and thirty over, and the young man, who heard himself haggled for twice in one year, does not look at you as you go.
The scribe's sum
A long narrow monk with a rag round his neck sits at a sloped desk with a ruled leaf in front of him and nothing written on it. He looks at your hands to see what they are carrying.

A lean-to writing house built for the light: four sloped desks under an open shutter, quills in a rack, horns of black and red ink, a calfskin stretched on a frame by the door; a long, narrow, chilblained scribe with a rag round his neck and a quill behind his ear turning from a blank ruled leaf toward the merchant; a boy ruling lines with a lead point.
Shut the door, the leaf is lifting. Do you carry calfskin? No? Then you have come to watch a man not write a book.
You. Good. I have ruled forty leaves on the strength of your promise. Tell me you have the skins.
Mainz wrote for the master's books in my teacher's day. Traiectum writes now. We send apologies. They are very well written.
I have a leaf of English verse about a storm under the sea. Do not ask where I got it. Ask what it means. Ten pennies.
You go up the coast. Is Ceolhelm still angry? No. Do not tell me. Of course he is.
The guest-master sent you up about the Frisians. I was nine. I do not tell it often. People want it to have been somebody's fault.
He asked after my hands? He did. Well. They are cold. Tell him they are cold, and that the leaf was always going to come back.
Sit through his reckoning of the master's book
Buy a copy of his leaf (10 d)
Give him the answer, and take the true leaf north
Ask what he saw at York, the year the Frisians ran

For the master's history of the English church: a hundred and thirty calves, red lead, orpiment, and a year. He has the year. He tells you what such a book fetches and from whom, and says he will write it if you will fetch the rest.

He writes it out without once looking at the leaf: sometimes I go, as men think not, under the rush of the waves, seeking the ocean's ground. He does not give the answer. He asks, as if it did not matter, whether you ever lie at the holy island.
He nods, shuts the shutter, and holds out the leaf itself, with a boot mark on its back and a fold where it lay in his shirt. Take it home to him, he says. Say I kept it flat.

He puts down the pen. He saw the tall one carried to the boat with his books, weeping, and a Frisian boy no older than himself pulled aboard by the hair. And the Frisian did not draw first: a child sees who draws. He writes it out fair for the archbishop's clerk, and looks at your steersman for some time.
The cellarer's scale

A wide door in the end of the long stone hall, with a beam scale hanging in it and a tally board chalked beside. The cellarer stands in the doorway so that nothing passes him uncounted, yourself included.

A wide doorway in the gable of a long stone hall, a beam scale hung in it and a chalked tally board on the jamb: a heavy-shouldered, red-faced monk with his cowl kilted up, keys and a tally stick at his belt and chalk on his fingers, filling the doorway; behind him casks, sacks, baled fleeces and grey cakes of wax in the cool dark.
God keep you. We do not sell here. Put it on the scale, and we shall see what the house can give you for your kindness.
You again, and the scale still honest from the last time. Come in out of the wind. What is it today?
Wheat at York is past what a man may ask with a straight face. Bring barley. Nobody is proud this year.
The scribe has told me a merchant is bringing calfskin. He has told the abbot. He has told the cat. If you have it, for the love of God put it on my scale.
I have a riddle of Abbot Hwaetberht's about a fish. I ask it of every man who sells me one. Nobody has yet paid for his supper with the answer.
The cattle are dying from here to the Tees. No calves, no books. The scribe thinks I arranged it.
Put a bundle of calfskin on his scale, for the scribe
Bring him barley at a price he can say in chapter
Ask him for the abbot's riddle of the fish
Put your goods on the scale and take what the house gives

He weighs the bundle in and writes nothing against it, on the abbot's word. The scribe carries the skins up the hill himself, two at a time, like new bread. Two barrels of salt salmon and thirty pennies come back the other way, with a standing order for more.

Five pennies the sack. He says the number aloud twice, to hear how it will sound before the brethren, and finds it will do. Then, since a fair man should have something over, he writes out the abbot's riddle of the fish for you, in Latin, and wishes you a reader.

He says it in Latin, counting the feet on his fingers, and then cuts it on a tablet so that you may carry it to somebody who can read. It is about a fish, he says. That much he will give away. The rest is the work.

He counts aloud while he talks, and stops talking when the scale swings. What the house gives is barley, wool, hides and salmon, in that order of willingness. It is full measure. He would be ashamed of anything else, and says so.
The old man's question

Six iron-bound chests stand at the end of the abbot's room, and under the window four boys sit with wax tablets on their knees. A very old monk with milky eyes turns his face toward your step and asks his question before you have crossed the floor.

The end of a painted stone room: six oak chests with iron bands, one open with books lying flat in their boards; under a small window four boys on a bench with wax tablets, and beside them a very old, bent, half-blind monk in a cowl too big for him, counting on his finger joints, his face turned toward the merchant in the doorway.
A merchant. Then you can count. If the moon is nine days old at noon, when is high water on our bar? Take your time. The boys never do.
I know the step. You are the one who answered about the tide. Sit by me. Is the boy well?
I was at the door when the master died. He finished the sentence first. People forget that part.
Two brothers from up the coast. One left us for the sea, and the sea took the other. I taught them both to count.
He stood there, on that board, and neither of us said it. It was well done. Go away now. I am an old man, and the dust is in my eyes.
Answer his question about the tide
Buy his riddles of the sun and of the moon (6 d)
Bring your lookout up the hill to him
Let the boys have their lesson

Your steersman works it on his fingers and you say it: a little after the sixth hour, and later tomorrow. The old man smiles at the wall. Near enough, he says. The master asked sailors too, and wrote down what they told him.
You say it, and four boys look hard at their tablets so as not to laugh. Wrong by half a tide, the old man says, kindly. Do not sail by that. Sail by your steersman, who is muttering behind you.
