Six pennies for the wax, he says, and nothing for the riddles, which were given to him. A boy writes while he recites: one about a thing that burns the living from far off and never touches them, and one about a thief who carries plunder home between his horns.

Beornwine comes as far as the door and no further. The old man says: you are standing on the board that creaks. You always did. Neither of them says the other thing. The boy reads a page aloud, slowly and truly, and afterwards rows as if the boat had been lightened.
He has already turned back to the bench. Seven and nineteen, he is saying, and again, until you can say it in your sleep. The boys say it. One of them watches you go as a prisoner watches a bird.
What the sea gave back

Ribs and strakes of broken ships stand out of the south sand at the river mouth, with gulls on them. A wiry fisherman is watching you look. He has something in his thatch, and has been deciding for some time whom to show it to.

The bar of a river mouth at low water under a windy sky: a long pale sand with the black ribs and strakes of wrecked ships standing out of it, gulls perched on them; on a southern headland the grassed walls of an old fort; in front a wiry, mud-legged fisherman with a sounding pole holding out a short stick cut with notches and a horn-handled knife to the merchant.
Their ships broke on the bar in a north-easter. I did not pray for them. I did not pray against them either.
The sea gave back a stick with cuts on it, and a knife with a handle of some horn I do not know. The monks cannot read the stick. Six pennies, or a sound net.
Your Northman looks at my stick the way a priest looks at a book. I do not like it. I should like to know what it says.
There is another thing the sea gave. He is in the old fort with a broken arm. My wife has fed him a month, against all sense. The reeve's men are asking along the shore.
The chief they caught alive. I shall not say what was done. The men who did it eat at my table.
Buy the stick and the knife (6 d)
Have your Northman read the stick
Take the wounded boy aboard by night
Walk the sand and buy nothing

He fetches them out of the thatch wrapped in a bit of net. The stick is as long as a hand, cut on two edges. The knife is good iron in a handle of pale horn, worn where a thumb has lain. He seems lighter for being rid of them.

He turns it over twice. It is a tally: so many head, so much silver by weight, and a man's mark. The horn of the knife is reindeer, he says, and men who count captives on a stick sell them at a market. He does not say which market. He would, to a bishop.

Fifteen, perhaps, grey with pain, and he does not make a sound when your men lift him over the gunwale. He knows whose tally the stick is. He knows much, for a boy, and tells it a word at a time as his arm mends. Your lookout will not sit on the same thwart for a month.

The wrecks are stripped to the ribs already: every rivet has gone to somebody's door. The fisherman walks with you as far as the old fort and then, for no reason he gives, turns you round and walks you back.
Knots on a string
A round, quick monk with his sleeves rolled meets you at the guest-house door with a ladle in his hand. At his belt hangs a string of knots, and his fingers are already on the next bare length of it.

A stone guest house near the water, painted plaster inside and one small window of coloured glass throwing red and blue spots on the floor: a round, cheerful monk with rolled sleeves and a linen cloth over his shoulder, a wooden ladle in one hand and a knotted string at his belt, waving the merchant to a bench by a long hearth; a dog asleep.
In, in, mind the step. There is barley and a bit of salmon. Now: where from, how long at sea, and what did you pass?
The same bench as before. You were asking after a boy, or a book. Sit. I have something for you.
One knot for every sail this year. That one is you. That thick one is three together, last summer. I do not like to tie thick ones.
A Frisian lay here before Whitsun. He said York's reeve asks every Frisian his father's name. Old blood, he said. He did not stay to eat.
The scribe up the hill was a boy at York that year. Ask him. He likes to be asked. Then he likes to refuse. Then he tells you.
Tynemouth buried a king two harvests back. That river mouth collects them.
Give him your ship news for his string
Ask what the Frisian meant by old blood
Sleep under the coloured window

He ladles while you talk and ties a knot when you have done. Then he pays in kind: who has landed this season, what they said of prices and kings, and which fisher will pilot a stranger over the bar for his supper.

Twenty years back, he says, a Frisian merchant killed a great man's son at York in a brawl, and every Frisian in the city ran for his ship. Nothing was ever paid. He points up the hill with the ladle. The scribe was a boy there then.
The house takes nothing for a bed. In the morning the one good window throws red and blue across your blanket, and the bell for the office comes down the hill before the gulls are up.
The apostles' day

It is the feast of Peter and Paul, and Saint Paul's own house keeps it with both choirs. After the Mass the abbot has you brought to the long hall, where the brothers eat in silence while one of them reads.

A long stone refectory floored in pink mortar: monks at benches along the walls eating in silence, one on a stool reading from a letter; at the upper end a lean grey-tonsured abbot in a darned cowl with a plain ash staff, the Frisian merchant seated beside him as a guest; small coloured windows; midsummer light.
You are welcome on the apostles' day. The house gives today and takes nothing. Tomorrow the cellarer will take, and you will find that he remembers.
What is being read is a letter. 'You live by the sea, from which this plague first came.' Master Alcuin wrote it to us. I have it read on feasts, so that we do not grow comfortable.
I ask every shipman one thing. If you see sails from the north, come back and say so before you sell. I ask it as a favour. I have nothing to order a merchant with.
You came back and told me truly what was on the sea. I have not forgotten it. The watch on the headland was kept that week because of you.
Tell him truly what you saw off the bar
Give a cask of wine for the altar, on the apostles' day
Eat in silence and listen to the reader

You tell him every sail between the Humber and the Tyne, and which of them you could not name. He listens to the end, thanks you, and sends a boy running to the south headland before the reader has turned his leaf.

The cask is carried up the hill by four brothers singing. The abbot thanks you first and then cannot say no, since it is a gift. Two barrels of the house's salmon come down to the boat that evening, because this house gives, and is given to.

Barley bread, eels, and a cup of the house's ale, with one voice going on over the scrape of spoons. You follow the Latin for whole sentences together. Your lookout, at the low end, follows all of it, and is seen to be doing so.
One chapter
The book is on the shelf: the master's history, in its boards. The scribe takes it down, finds the place with one finger, and looks at you over the top of it.

An open book chest and a heavy book in wooden boards held open on a monk's forearm: a long narrow scribe with one finger on a line, eyebrows raised at the merchant; boys with wax tablets on a bench under the window behind; dust in a shaft of light.
The City of the Legions. The battle, and the monks of Bangor cut down at their prayers. Second book, second chapter. He wants only the part about himself? Priests.
One leaf, both sides, a fair hand. Twenty pennies, or a cake of wax. Or your runaway can copy it on the boys' bench for nothing, if his hand has not gone to the oar.
For the man who took Ceolhelm his leaf, I rule the lines for nothing. The writing still costs. I am not made of ink.
Pay him twenty pennies for the leaf
Pay him a cake of wax
Set your lookout to copy it on the boys' bench

He writes it in a morning, in a hand as even as a ploughed field, and reads it over to you so that you will know what you carry: the heathen king, the prayers on the hill, twelve hundred dead. Keep it flat, he says. They all say that.
He smells the wax, pinches it, and puts it inside his habit before the cellarer can see. The leaf is done by evening, with a small red letter at the head that was not in the bargain.
It takes him two days and much muttering. The scribe corrects four words, sniffs at the ruling, and says the hand is still there under the blisters. The leaf is yours, and cost you only the days.
The master's day

It is the night of the master's day, and you have kept the vigil at Bede's grave beside a quiet priest of Durham. Past midnight there was a small sound of iron on stone from the north porch. Now, before light, he is down at the boats with a linen bag that is no longer flat.

The grey hour before dawn on a mudflat under a low rise with two old stone churches: a spare young priest in a good black cloak standing by the merchant's boat with a pilgrim's staff, both arms round a full linen bag held against his chest; fishers' houses dark behind; a last candle in a church window.
God's peace, merchant. I start before light; I walk better in the cool. Is that your boat? I should be glad of a passage up the river, toward the Durham road.
The bag? A saint should not lie under a roof the rain comes through. I only say what anyone would say.
When the brethren at Durham ask where the master rests, I tell them: he who knows about Cuthbert knows about Bede.
Give him the passage and ask nothing
Ask him, at the boats, what is in the bag
Wake the fishers and the people at the vigil

He sits in the bow with the bag on his knees and both arms round it, and says the office under his breath the whole way up the river. On the thwart, when he has gone up the bank, lies a purse with ten shillings in it. He never comes to Gyrwe again.

He looks at you for some time, and then at the fishers' houses, which are dark. Then he tells you all of it, quietly, as a man makes his confession to a stranger on a road. You may tell it, he says, when I am dead. He walks to Durham.

Lights, dogs, forty country people in the churchyard, and a priest of Durham standing very still with a bag. Nobody lays a hand on him. He sets it down on the grave himself and goes away up the river road on foot. The master lies at Gyrwe still. The people of the Slake call you theirs; Durham's door is another matter.
The abbess asks
A tall spare woman in a white veil is waiting in the north porch of the church where the kings lie. She has walked up from the guest house to meet you, which the cellarer says she does for nobody.

The north porch of a small lime-washed stone church on a high headland, sea far below: a tall, spare, weathered woman of fifty in a dark gown and a white veil pinned with two plain bronze pins, keys at her girdle, standing with folded hands before the merchant; inside, lamps over two long grave slabs.
You came from the north, or from the south? If the north, sit. Tell me what you saw with your own eyes, and leave out what you heard.
The merchant. Good. The cellarer says your count was right the last time. Is the island's bishop still on his island?
They saw the sails from the kings' rock and did not come down. I ask myself who would come down for us. So I have a question for the bishop of the island, and no boat.
My question is still at sea, then. Good. A question in a careful man's keeping is better than an answer in a fool's.
You have been to the island. I see it. Do not tell me in the porch. Come inside, where the kings can hear it too.
The scribe is copying and the kings stay where they are. I have decided once, and I do not say perhaps. Thank you for carrying both halves of it.
One of your men is holding his arm like a broken wing. Send him up to me. I have a small knife and thirty years of practice.
Tell her what you saw with your own eyes
Take her question to the bishop on the island
Give her Higbald's answer
Send your hurt man up to her
She asks plain questions and waits for the whole of each answer: how many ships, how low in the water, which way they went. She thanks you by name. She has asked the cellarer for it beforehand.

It is one sentence, and she has you say it back: has he moved the saint, and would he, in her place, move a king? She gives you nothing written. A letter can be read by the wrong man, she says. You cannot.

A book can be written twice and a bone cannot. She has the three lines read over twice beside the long slabs. Then she sends for the scribe and tells her to begin tomorrow on a second copy of the house's own book of Pope Gregory. A bolt of the house's cloth goes down to your boat, and a place by name on the guest bench.

She cleans it with wine she can ill spare, opens what needs opening with a knife no longer than a finger, and binds it in linen. He is not to pull an oar for six days. She says it to you, not to him, since you are the one who will be tempted.
What the sea gave

Above the tide line under the East Cliff lies a sea chest with a foreign lock, bleached, and stove in at one corner. The boatman who walks this shore every morning is sitting on it, waiting for somebody who can read.

A narrow sand beach under a leaning cliff after a gale, drifts of black weed and broken timber: a short, bow-legged boatman with a face like tanned hide sitting on a stove-in sea chest with a foreign iron lock, holding out a leaf of writing in a waxed cloth to the merchant; a knife and a comb laid on the lid beside him; roofs of the house far above.
The sea gives. It gave me a cask once, and once a man. The cask was the better company. This morning, after the gale, it gave me this.
A knife. A comb. And a leaf with writing on it, dry as a bone in a waxed cloth. I cannot read it. Is it worth ale, or silver?
The nun who keeps the writing house would know. She would also keep it. So I am asking you first.
Pay him fairly for the leaf (8 d)
Tell him it is worth a cup of ale, and take it
Carry it up the cliff and let the nun read it first
Leave the chest and the leaf where they lie

Eight pennies, and he bites one. The leaf is English verse in a small crowded hand: sometimes my master sends me under the earth, and I shake the halls; sometimes I drive the flint-grey flood against the cliffs. It asks who can still that. It does not say.

He takes the ale. He is not a fool: he watches how carefully you fold the cloth round a thing worth one cup. Next time you ask him the state of the bar he will tell you, slowly, and it will cost more.

She reads it aloud, once in English and once slowly for a Frisian ear. That is Lindisfarena's hand, she says, and Ceolhelm's ruling: he always crowds the last line. She makes a copy for the house and gives the leaf back. She will not say the answer. She says the leaf itself says who is asked.
He shrugs, and puts the leaf back inside his shirt, where it will be safe from everything but him. The sea gives, he says. It does not say what for.
Black and bright

On the flat grey rock under the cliff, women and children are turning over a fresh fall of shale. A wiry man with a rope of twisted hide over his shoulder holds out a black stone, and waits to see what you will do with it.

A wide floor of flat grey rock at low water under a wet, leaning cliff: a fresh fall of shale and clay with women and children picking through it; a wiry, wind-burned man with a coiled hide rope over one shoulder and a short iron pick holding out a lump of black stone to the merchant; a small fire of driftwood; kittiwakes.
Jet? Hold out your hand. Feel the weight: light as wood. Now rub it on your sleeve, and pick up that straw with it.
You know the tests. Then you know I am not selling you the cliff. The big piece is at the bottom of the bag. It always is.
A Frankish lord wants black stone for a cross in his chapel? Then he wants the old seam, the hard bright kind. It costs more. A lord would notice the other.
The cellar offers the king's brass for it. You pay in iron and salt. So you get the big piece.
My grandmother burned a crumb of it on the hearth every spring. The smoke drives off snakes. We have no snakes. So it works.
Learn the three tests from him
Buy a sack at the gatherers' price (16 d)
Pick the best of the old seam for the count's chapel (30 d)
Watch the gatherers work the fall

True jet is light in the hand. Rubbed warm, it lifts a straw, as amber does. And a crumb on the fire burns and smells of coal. He makes you do all three, twice, with a lump of the heavy dull stuff beside it for shame. If a man offers you black stone that is heavy, he says, he is selling you the cliff.
He fills the sack from three different bags so that you can see he is not hiding the dull ones at the bottom, and ties it with a knot the cellar will know is his.

He goes up the rope himself for it and is gone the whole of the ebb. What he brings down is hard, close-grained and black as a wet night, enough for a cross a hand high and beads besides. Tell your lord, he says, that a man hung over the sea for that.

They turn each slab with a knife point and know the stone by its edge before it is free. A child finds a coiled thing in the rock like a sleeping snake and is told to put it back. The tide gives them as long as a Mass, and then takes the floor away.
Black stone for the count

The count's steward has the tally stick with your name on it in one hand. With the other he turns a lump of black stone to the light of the hall door, rubs it on his sleeve, and watches a straw jump to it.

The doorway of a Frankish count's timber hall: a careful, grey-haired steward holding a notched tally stick in one hand and a lump of polished black stone in the other, a straw clinging to it; the Frisian merchant before him with an open sack; a clerk looking on from a bench; morning light off the river.
The chaplain read it to my lord from the English priest's book: a black stone that burns, and draws straws like amber. My lord said: get me some. From where? That, he said, is why I keep a steward.
This would stand for the errand you owe in place of silver. I should cut the notch away while you watch. A stick remembers. A steward only says that he does.
You owe no errand, and you bring my lord a thing he asked for at table and forgot by morning. That is either a gift or a price. Say which, before I thank you.
Hand it over as the errand you owed
Give it as a gift to the count's chapel
Name a price for it
Say the stone is not yet picked over, and keep it

He cuts the errand's notch off the stick with three strokes and puts the shaving in your hand. The stone goes to the count's goldsmith for a cross, a hand high. My lord will say it was his own idea to send you, the steward says. Let him.

He weighs the word gift for a moment and finds it sound. The count hears of it at table. For a season the toll man on the dam counts your bales a little less carefully, which is how a lord says thank you without saying it.

Sixty pennies, he says, since it is the only black stone on the Rhine and you both know it. He pays from the count's box and writes it down. A thing paid for, he remarks, is a thing nobody need remember.
He gives it back without argument. It has come from the edge of the world, he says. It can lie another week in a sack.
When the harp comes round
It is a feast night, and the guest house keeps the old custom: the harp goes from hand to hand down the bench, and each one gives what he has. It is three places away from you, and coming.

One room with a hearth in the middle of the floor and benches along both walls, full on a feast night: a small harp being passed from a laughing monk to a carter; three places further on the Frisian merchant looking at it with alarm; by the door an old, bent cowherd in an undyed hooded cloak getting quietly to his feet; peat smoke and firelight.
Every man gives something on a feast. A song, a story, a verse of the Psalms. I gave mine. They cheered. I think they were glad it was over.
I must see to the cattle. The red cow is near her time. She has been near her time for fifty years, whenever that thing comes down the bench.
A hundred years back a cowherd of this house got up at just this moment and went out to the byre. You know what came of that. No? Then you have not been here on a feast before.
Take the harp, and give them a Frisian rowing chant
Remember your boat, as the cowherd did his cattle, and go out
Pass the harp on, and set the bench a riddle

You cannot play the thing, so you beat time on its frame and give them the stroke-chant your men pull to: forty verses, most of them about the steersman's mother. The bench roars the burden back by the third. The cellarer says it is not a psalm, and asks for it again.

The old cowherd is sitting in the straw by the byre door. This is the place, he says, and says the song through, flat as a tally: now we must praise the keeper of heaven, the might of the Maker and the thought of his mind. He will say it as often as it takes you to learn.

You hand the harp to a carter and give them one out of your own chest. Two pilgrims guess wrong. The nun from the writing house, who should not be listening at the door, guesses right and is cross with herself for saying so aloud.
The cellar door

At the top of the cliff path there is a half-door with a beam scale hung in it, and the wind getting at everything. A round-shouldered brother with a tally stick is turning a black gaming piece over and over in his fingers.

A long low building of stone footings and timber at the head of a cliff path, a half-door on the seaward side with a beam scale hung in it: bolts of grey and brown cloth, sacks of wool, a basket of rough black stones, a tub of salted salmon; a round-shouldered, greying monk with a tally stick turning a black jet gaming piece in his fingers; wind tearing at his habit.
Thanks be to God, a sail. Come up to the fire. Broth first, prices after, and the board after that, if you play.
I kept your place on the bench and your last move in my head. You were losing. Sit down.
The king's coin will buy you a loaf here and a laugh at Lundenwic. Take cloth. Cloth is the same in every tongue.
Wax is dear this year. I am told the bees of Francia have turned heathen and keep it for themselves.
They pay us in brass now, by the bucket. I weigh the bucket. Sometimes I weigh it empty, to cheer myself.
Sell him a cask of wine for the house's cloth
Play him at the board for two sacks of wool (stake 6 d)
Take the writing house's order for colours
Take the broth and the prices

Four bolts for the cask, grey and brown, close-woven on the house's own looms. He says the price once and then talks about something else, and when you look again the cask has already gone up to the church.

He opens as he always opens and you have seen it before. When his king is shut in he looks at the board for a long time, and then at the door, in case the abbess is passing. Two sacks. He carries them down himself, to have a reason to ask for a return game.
He has every opening by heart and a jet king that seems to slide out of traps by itself. Six pennies. He drops them in the alms box in front of you, so that it is not gaming, and grins.

Red lead, and the yellow that looks like gold, he reads off a wax tablet in a hand that is not his. Two pouches within the year, and the house will pay well over the common price, since the nun who wrote the list will give him no peace until it comes.

Barley broth with a little fish in it, and then every price on the coast with a number in each second sentence: what the last three ships asked, who paid it, and who should not have. A bell from the church cuts him short in the middle of a fleece.
The cowherd at the wall

On the landward side of the house an old man leans on a pasture wall, watching small black cattle steam in the morning. He does not turn round. He has known for some time that you were coming up the field.

A long turf-walled byre with its door away from the wind, a walled pasture running back toward heather: small black cattle steaming in early light, and an old, lean, bent cowherd in a hooded cloak the colour of his cows leaning on the wall with a polished hazel stick, a wooden cup at his belt; the merchant coming up the field behind him.
A shipman. Then you will be wanting hides, and I shall be wanting news. Lean on the wall. The wall does not mind.
The red cow calved since you were here. That is my news. Yours had better be longer.
It was this byre. He lay down there by the door, and a man in a dream said: sing me the beginning of things.
Every calf I rear, the nun wants its skin. I tell them at birth: you will be a psalm. Be proud.
You have the song now. Say it at any fire on this coast and they will move up for you. Do not sing it. I never did, and it has lasted.
Buy hides at the byre's price (20 d)
Sit in the straw and have him say the song
Lean on the wall and give him your news
Two bundles, salted and rolled, for ten pennies each. The cellarer would have asked fifteen and called it charity. The old man says nothing about the cellarer. He does not need to.

He says it nine lines through, flat, with a long wait before the last word of each. Then again. By the fourth time you have it. I have slept in this straw fifty years, he says, and nobody came. I think heaven had heard my voice already.
He listens with his eyes on the cattle and asks one question at the end, about the price of salt. Then he tells you there will be wind by evening: the cows are lying with their backs to the sea.
The priests' farm

On the roofless headland one cell is thatched again, with a patch of beans beside it and a man's voice inside singing an office alone. Below, by the river, the Dane who holds the land is mending a plough. He has seen you look up.

A windy headland of roofless stone cells with nettles in the doorways, one cell newly thatched with a smoke hole and a bean patch; below it on the river flat a thick-set, red-bearded Danish farmer in a blue tunic kneeling by a plough, looking up at the merchant; boats drawn up bow to the land; larks.
There is a priest up among the stones. He does no harm. He prays for my barley, my wife says. It came up, so let him.
Some of my neighbours think those stones would build a good hall. I have not said yes. I have not said no. I am a farmer. I wait to see what grows.

York has a baptised king now, and an archbishop again. They would send me chrism and a hand bell, if a man the settlers trust would stand for me. I have had no bell these fifteen years. I knock two stones.
The bell is hung. I stood outside the wall on the day, with my arms folded, to the end. Nobody can say I went in.
Pay for the bell from York, and swear surety for the priest (90 d)
Carry dressed stone down to the river for the neighbours, for pay
Trade with Ketil, give the priest alms, and take no side (6 d)
Buy your jet at the booths and go

You swear it at the river before Ketil and four of his neighbours, with your hand on your own gunwale, since nobody could agree on a holier thing: the priest will take no man's land and curse no man's plough. The bell comes by the next York boat. After that Ketil's kin speak for your house at every settlers' meeting on this coast, and a booth stance by the river has your mark cut on its post.

Three days of it, with the boat low in the water: squared red blocks, a window head, a slab with a cross that somebody turns face down before it is loaded. A hundred and fifty pennies' weight of cut silver. The singing in the thatched cell stops while you work, and begins again when you have gone.

Six pennies in the priest's bowl and a fair price for Ketil's fish. Neither man thinks the worse of you. Neither will remember your name in a year, which in a country lately shared out by the rope is not the worst thing.
Ketil sells from a trestle between two boat sheds and cuts his change off a silver arm ring with a chisel. The sea here is not bad, he says as you push off, for a sea.
The hearths on the edge

A woman works an upright loom in a doorway on the lip of the headland, the clay weights knocking. Behind her house the grass stops and the sea begins. Her son is mending a net badly, and looking at your boat far below.

A timber house on the very lip of a headland, smoke from its roof and a heap of shells by the door: a woman at an upright loom in the doorway with clay weights hanging from the warp, and beside her a lanky youth with a half-mended net on his knees staring down past the cliff edge at a small boat on the sand far below; nothing behind them but sea and sky.
He climbs for eggs like his father, and he looks at ships like nobody in this family. The cliff took his father. I suppose the sea is no worse a neighbour.
I can hang on a rope over that all morning and never look down. I can pull an oar. I cannot read the water yet. I can learn it.
The house's cloth goes out by the cellar door with the cellarer's share on it. Mine goes out by this door. Feel that. That is two winters of evenings.
We look north in the mornings now. A long hull where no trade is: the abbess has asked every hearth to send a child running if we see one.
Take the boy on as a hand (6 d to his mother)
Buy her own cloth at her own door (14 d)
Ask what ships have passed

She takes the six pennies, counts them into a pot under the loom, and does not look up when he goes. He is down the cliff path before you are, and sick before the river bar, and by the next port he can tie everything your steersman can and one knot he cannot.
A bolt of close grey twill for fourteen pennies, four under what the cellar asks. She folds it herself and tells you which side goes outward, as if a Frisian had never seen cloth.

From this door, she says, you see every sail between the two nesses. A fat trader for the Humber at dawn. Two fishing boats from the north. Nothing with stripes. She says the last part as a woman says a short prayer.
Forty pigs

Under a lean-to of turf and old roof tiles, grey pigs of lead are stacked like loaves, each as long as a forearm. The man who sits there has grey in the creases of his hands. He watches you look at the stack, and waits for you to try to lift one.

A lean-to of turf and broken Roman roof tiles against the foot of a great red stone wall: grey pigs of lead stacked like loaves, a two-wheeled cart with a broken felloe, thin grey-dusted grass; a broad, stooped man of forty in a scorched leather apron sitting on the stack with a short iron bar across his knees, watching the merchant bend to lift a pig.
You are looking at the pigs. Everyone does. Lift one before you ask the price. It saves talk.
The boat that carries more than she looks. I kept six pigs back for you, in case you came.
A Frankish abbot wants lead for his church roofs. He is King Offa's friend. His own king has shut the ports, so his roofs leak. That is kings for you.
That stick is the abbot's token, cut two summers back. Forty pigs. Ten pennies a pig to any man who will try the crossing, and half his gain sworn to me.
Read me that again. 'Forbidden to merchants.' English merchants. English ships. You are neither. Nine pennies, then, since you bring me law as well as silver.
The ports are open? Then the price is up a penny a pig since this morning. Do not look at me so. You brought the news yourself.
You carry ten pigs of mine on your word. I think about them at night. Lead is honest. I am finding out about Frisians.
Six are set aside behind the cart with your mark chalked on them. Digger's price. You kept an oath to a man with no kin to enforce it.
Buy six pigs at ten pennies (60 d)
Show him the scribe's line, and buy six at nine (54 d)
Swear him half the gain, and take ten pigs on your word
Lift one, and ask where it comes from

He counts your silver on his fingers and never loses the count. Then he shows your men how to stow the pigs, low along the keel and wedged with turf. If she sinks, he says, at least you will know why.

He cannot read it, so the priest is fetched to read it, and reads it twice. Forbidden to English merchants. The lead man looks at your cloak and your boat and does a slow sum. A Frisian hull is not an English one. Nine pennies.

You swear it with your hand on the stack, before the ale-wife and the priest, who are the witnesses this place has: ten pennies a pig, and half of whatever the ten fetch over that, brought back to this bank. He helps to stow them himself, and watches the boat out of sight.

It is as heavy as a calf and as cold. From the hills, he says, by the old workings, where the Romans cut their names into theirs. He has a saying of his grandfather's about the stuff, a hard one, about a thing dug out of its home and purified with fire, that now drives men wide over the plains. He gives it to you to chew on.
Half the gain
The lead man is sitting by his stack, as he always is. He does not ask what the ten pigs fetched. He looks at your boat, to see how she rides, and then at your purse.

The lead stack under the red wall again, ten pigs fewer: the stooped lead man on his feet for once with a long notched stick in his hand, facing the merchant; a thin, grey-tonsured priest in a patched brown tunic standing a little apart with his hands folded, looking up at a small stone church on the cliff.
Ten pigs went down this river on your word. I have counted the days since on a stick. It is a long stick.
Ten pennies a pig was mine already. Half of what they fetched over that is mine by your oath. Say the number. I shall believe it. That is what an oath is for.
I ask nothing. I only mention that the rain comes through over the altar, and that six pigs beaten flat would cover the worst of it.
Count out his hundred pennies and his half, truly (130 d)
Pay him, and buy six pigs more for the priest's roof (190 d)
Tell him they fetched little, and pay the hundred only (100 d)
Say the silver is still at sea

A hundred for the pigs and thirty for his half of the gain. He counts it twice on his fingers and breaks the long stick over his knee. From now on, he says, six pigs are always kept back for your house at the digger's price, whoever else comes asking.

The oath is paid to the penny, and six pigs go up the cliff on the ox cart instead of down the river. The lead man beats them flat himself, for nothing, since he promised that roof at his wife's burial. The priest says that your house may lie in his ground when its time comes, and that he hopes it will be late.

He takes the hundred and looks at you for the time it takes to lift a pig. Lead is honest, he says. It weighs what it weighs. He does not keep six back for you again, and the ale-wife, who was a witness, charges you for the next cup before she pours it.
He nods slowly and cuts another notch. The priest goes back up to his church and moves the bucket under the drip.
The warm wall
Inside the south gate a Roman wall stands higher than any tree, with a roof of thatch slung across one corner. Under it are a hearth, three benches, and a woman who looks at every face twice.

The corner of a towering Roman bath wall with a round arch in it and a thatch roof slung across: a hearth, three benches, casks on a floor of small coloured squares; a strong-armed woman in a madder-red gown and linen head-cloth, keys and a wooden dipper at her belt, looking hard at the merchant's face; swallows going in and out overhead.
Sit by the warm wall. Romans built it to heat water. I use it to keep ale from the frost. Who are you, and who answers for you?
Your bench is where you left it. I remember what you drank, what you paid, and what you said about the weather. You were wrong about the weather.
That lookout of yours owes me for a cup from his first night here. I have not forgotten his face. I mean to collect it for the rest of his life.
A Dorestat skipper lay here one summer. Thiadbod. He paid in clipped pennies and asked too closely about the lead. I kept one of the pennies, to show.
It is a fast. The priest eats here on what the rule allows, and a little that it does not. I keep his fast honest and his belly off his backbone.
King Offa is digging a ditch to keep the Welsh out. My sister's man digs on it. He says the Welsh come at night and help, the other way.
Pay your lookout's cup (1 d)
Hire the Dee man she vouches for (6 d)
Ask what Thiadbod wanted with the lead
Drink, and let her look at you twice

One penny, on the board, with the lookout standing behind you looking at his feet. She takes it, bites it, and tells him his face is clear in this house. She seems almost sorry to have nothing left to hold over him.

A quiet man with a net-mender's hands, who has drunk here ten years and never once owed. He knows the river to the sea and the Welsh shore beyond it. She tells him, in front of you, what she will do if he comes back with a bad word of your boat.

He wanted to know who had asked before him, she says, and what the abbot's token looked like, and whether the lead man could read. Then he went away to think. A man who goes away to think about forty pigs of lead means to come back when nobody else can buy.

The ale is fresh from the new moon's brewing, and the wall at your back is as warm as a horse. Two Welshmen came over the ford with honey this week, she says, and went back with salt. That is the market. Do not tell the king. He will want a toll.
A leaf about this place

The priest of Saint John's is waiting at the church door on the red cliff. He has heard a keel on the river, and he has a question he has been keeping for the first man who looks as if he has seen a book.

A small stone church on a red cliff above a shining river, built of blocks from the grassed-over oval ruin beside it, jackdaws wheeling: at the door a thin, grey-tonsured priest near fifty in a patched brown tunic with a wooden cross on a thong, hands half raised toward the merchant coming up the path.
God keep you. A sail on this river is a thing to write down, if I had anything to write on. Come in out of the wind.
The Frisian again. I said a Mass for your keel at Candlemas. It seems to have held.
They say the priest Bede wrote of this city: legions, a battle, monks cut down at their prayers. I have never seen the words. Do you ever lie at a house where his book is kept?
You have not been north yet. No. I only ask. I have asked every tide for a year. It is a habit now, like the office.
That is a leaf. In your hand. Do not unfold it in this wind. Come inside. No. Wait. Let me wash my hands.
There is lead over the altar now, and the rain goes elsewhere. I say your house's name at the offering. The Welsh who cross the ford have begun to say it too, wrongly.
It is Saint John's own day, and the church is as full as it ever is: nine households, a goat, and whoever has come over the ford. No bale is opened until I have sung.
Saint Cuthbert's church robbed, and the brothers killed? Say it again, slowly. I must tell it to forty people, and I will not get it wrong.
Promise to have the leaf made in the north
Put the leaf in his hands
Let him read Alcuin's letter out of your chest
Ask his blessing, and give him the news

He tells you what he was told as a boy, so that you will know the place when a scribe finds it: the City of the Legions, a heathen king, monks on a hill. He can pay in prayers and a burial plot. He says it without shame. It is what he has.

He reads it aloud at the church door, a line at a time, in English: the heathen king, the monks praying against him on the hill, twelve hundred dead. Nobody under the wall knew they lived anywhere that was in a book. He will teach you the Latin letters for it, he says, a little at each visit, until he dies or you can read.

He reads it standing, with his lips moving, and then again sitting down. A master's own Latin, he says, and only at second hand from the master. He asks leave to copy four lines onto the wall plaster with a nail, having nothing else, and you give it.

He blesses the boat from the cliff, since he does not like the path down, and then asks which saint's day it was when you left home. He works your whole voyage out by feasts, and is right to within a day.
The sands of the Dee

A hide boat lies upside down on stakes like a black bowl, and beside it an Irishman is greasing a seam with mutton fat. A lean man with a notched sounding pole is looking at where you have left your boat, with the scorn of a man who is always asked the same thing.

A shelf of red mud and shingle under a red stone wall with a gap where a gate was: a hide boat upturned on stakes like a black bowl, a cheerful Irish seaman greasing its seam; a lean, weathered pilot in a sealskin cap, muddy to the knee, leaning on a notched sounding pole and looking sourly at the merchant's boat; evening light down the river.
You came up on the flood with nobody aboard who knows this river. Either God loves you or the sands were asleep. Next time, ask for me.
The Frisian. Still afloat. The channel has moved a boat's length since you saw it. I say so before you ask.
Keep to the Wirral shore going out, close enough to count the cows. The Welsh side is all sand, and the sand moves at night.
In my country there is a bird that is never an egg. It grows on a floating timber, beak down in the salt water, and one day it flies. I have a verse on it, if you like a hard thing.
Past the point there is a beach where boats have traded since before the Romans. No king's man stands there. I never told you so.
Hire Osfrith to take you down on the ebb (3 d)
Take the Irishman's verse of the bird
Ask him plainly about the beach past the point
Go down the river without him

He stands in the bow with his pole and never looks at the water, only at the cows on the Wirral shore. He has been wrong about these sands twice in his life, he says, and names both days. This is not one of them.

He says it over in English that he has plainly got from a monk: my beak was held fast, and I under the water, sunk in the flood, and in the sea I grew. He will not say what it is. He eats them on fast days, he says, since anything born of wood and water must be fish.

On the tip of Wirral, he says, where the sand is hard and a boat can lie at any tide. Men have bartered there since before anybody wrote anything down. No board, no reeve, no witness. He never told you so. He says that twice.

Your steersman keeps the cows close and the lead going, and you are over the bar by the last of the ebb with a hand's width of water to spare. Osfrith, on the bank, pretends not to have been watching.

You take the ground on a bank that was not there last year, and sit on it through a cold tide with the boat on her bilge and the men wet to the waist. Osfrith rows out at the flood, says nothing at all, and takes your bow line.
Across the ford

At the crossing a flat boat hangs on a rope of twisted hide, and cattle stand in the shallows. A man from the far bank has a crock of honey on a plank laid across two Roman column drums. He holds up two fingers, and then points at your salt.

A river crossing with a flat ferry on a hide rope and cattle standing in the shallows, a stepped red cliff on the far bank: in front, a plank across two Roman column drums with a crock of honey on it, a dark, wiry herdsman in a rough cloak holding up two fingers to the merchant, who has a sack of salt at his feet.
Two salt, one honey. You see? I have your words for the things that matter: salt, honey, cow, no.
Your king digs a ditch from sea to sea so that he need not look at us. It is a great honour. Nobody ever dug so much for a friend.
The priest sends over the sea for a leaf about our dead. We need no leaf. We have the names by heart, and a different count.
So the English book says twelve hundred. We say more, and we say their names. I should like to hear how it is told on your side. Once.
Give two sacks of salt for a crock of honey
Bring him over to hear the leaf read
Bargain on your fingers for what he has

He tastes the salt, you taste the honey, and it is done on fingers with no tongue between you. He carries the sacks over on his own back at the low stones, and waves once from the far bank without turning round.

He stands at the church door with his cap in his hand while the priest reads it through. Then he says his own people's count, and seven of the names, slowly, and the priest writes them in the margin of the leaf with a nail. Two bundles of hides come over the ford next morning. Nobody asked for them.
Honey, a cheese, and a hide with the hair on. He wants salt, an iron knife, and to know whether the king's ditch has reached the sea yet. You sell him nothing and tell him nothing, and part friends.
The waste city

There is smoke inside the red walls, where nobody has lived since the Romans. A Danish army has ridden across the whole breadth of the English lands in one march and shut itself in. Outside, the English have burned every stack and driven off every cow for a day's ride. Both sides have seen your sail.

A ruined square fortress of red stone on a ridge above a river, smoke of many fires rising inside it and armed men on the broken wall; the fields around burned black, a column of English horsemen driving cattle away; on the river below, the merchant's small boat with a bearded Dane hailing it from the bank and an English rider hailing it from the other.
We have walls, a river and silver. We have no corn. The English burned it, and what they did not burn their horses ate. Name a weight of silver for a sack. I shall not haggle. I shall remember.
Anything you land under that wall feeds the men who burned half Mercia. Land it on this bank, and the ealdorman pays the king's price, and you go home with your boat.
An empty boat. Then you are no use and no harm. Go down on the ebb, and tell them in the west that we are hungry and in a bad temper.
Sell your wheat under the wall, for silver by weight
Land it on the English bank at the king's price
Lie in the river mouth until it is over

They weigh it out in cut arm rings and Frankish pennies, thirty to the sack, and carry the wheat up through the broken gate on spear shafts. It is five times what any honest market gives. The English on the far bank cannot reach you. They can see you, and they know the cut of a Frisian sail.

Eight pennies the sack, in good pennies, and a thegn's word that the king's reeves on this coast will hear which boat it was. From the wall somebody shoots an arrow that falls a long way short, more as an opinion than an attack.

You sit behind the island in the river mouth and watch the smoke for three days. When the year turns the army goes into Wales for want of food, and the red walls stand empty again, with ash trees in them, as they have for four hundred years.
The reeve's board

Where the new wall comes down to the river a trestle stands under a penthouse roof, with a balance, an ale measure and a rail of lead tags on cords. Two reeves' men sit behind it, the king's and the earl's, and do not much like each other.

A trestle under a penthouse roof where a new red stone wall meets a river: a balance, a measure for ale, a peg rail hung with lead tags on cords; behind it a stout reeve in a green cloak with a round silver brooch and a thinner, sourer man beside him; porters carrying bales up from a landing past the board; a Dublin ship with a striped sail lying off.
Whose leave did you come in by? Say the king's, and I will believe you once. Four pennies a load when you go, and we are friends.
I know the boat. Lie where you lay before. If there are marten skins aboard, I see them before anyone. As before.
Marten skins. Then I look first. What the king does not want, the earl may want. What neither wants, you may sell.
Open no bale between Saturday's noon and Monday's light. God rests then. The bishop's man does not.
The king was here with every ship he owns, and six kings came and swore to him. I counted six. Ask me again in ten years and hear how many.
Your house knows the beach past the point. Every old house does. Forty shillings from the man who lands skins there. I find them all in the end.
Declare the load and pay the custom
Show him a timber of marten skins before anyone sees it
Land your skins on the beach past the point instead

He recites the custom like a prayer he has stopped hearing, counts your loads, and hangs a lead tag on each cord. Go in peace, he says, and come back the same way. It is the kindest thing he says to anybody.

He blows into the fur, counts the forty skins on their cord, and takes the timber for the king at the king's price, which is a little under the market's and paid at once. A man who shows his skins first, he says, pays his four pennies to a friend.

On the hard sand at the tip of Wirral a man with a Norse name and an Irish mother weighs out a hundred and fifty pennies for the timber and asks nothing. No board, no tag, no four pennies. Also no witness, which you remember all the way up the river.

The reeve's man is sitting on the dune when you come ashore, eating bread and cheese. He knows the beach better than you do. Forty shillings by the custom of the port, the skins held until it is paid, and your name said at the board before the earl's man.
The wall and the shore

Carts of stone and lime go past the Lady's hall all day to the wall. Inside, a woman with lime dust on her shoes asks short questions. On the Wirral shore, a day down the river, a tired sea-lord buys hides, and asks lightly how high the south wall stands these days.

A new-thatched timber hall inside a red fortress wall under repair, carts of stone and lime passing, spears in a rack by the door: in the doorway a straight-backed woman of forty in a plain dark gown with a gold-wire border and a white head-cloth, lime dust on her shoes, questioning the merchant; over the wall, far off, the sand shore of an estuary with ships drawn up.
You came by water past Wirral. How many ships on the north shore, hauled up or afloat? Then we will talk about your cargo.
The Irish among them are christened men. I have a word I want carried to those: that they are remembered, and by whom.
The Lady gave us land by the sea. Sand, mostly. She is generous with sand. Sell me hides and ale, and do not count my ships while you do it.
You sold to me and told her nothing she could use. A man like that is welcome on this beach, and on one or two others I could name.
They came at the wall. We poured the town's ale on them, boiling, and when they put up hides we threw down the hives. I have not yet paid the bee-keepers. Remind me.
Count the ships for the Lady, and carry her word to the Irish
Sell hides on the shore, and tell her nothing she can use
Sell to both, and carry word for both
Stay out of the river until it is over

You give her the number, hauled up and afloat, and she thanks you by name. Her word goes down the river in your head and is said quietly on the shore to men with Irish mothers. A plot on the river street is yours for the building, she says, and you will not pay at her gate while she lives.

Irish silver by weight, twenty-five to the bundle, and a seat by a driftwood fire among people who came away from Dublin with nothing. The old lord tells you where on the point a boat may lie at any tide with no reeve to see her. The Lady's hall is closed to you until she is dead.

The Lady hears a number of ships, and the old lord hears the height of a wall. Each pays. Each has other men who count, and finds your sums a little different from theirs. It is the most silver of any road, and the fewest friends.

You trade along the Welsh shore for a season instead. One morning there is smoke over the red walls, and by evening it is gone. The tale that comes down the river afterwards has boiling ale in it, and bees.
Feet first

Just inside the gap in the great bank a brother stands with his sleeves rolled, beside a wooden tub. He is going to wash your feet whether you like it or not. Behind him the smell of meat is coming out of a house where, by the day, there should be none.

A gap in a turf bank as high as a house, a long wattle-and-thatch guest house just inside it: in front a wooden tub and a stout, red-faced monk with rolled sleeves and a linen towel over one shoulder, beckoning the merchant to sit; a pilgrim asleep in the doorway with his boots on; tall stone crosses beyond; green island light.
Feet first, friend, then news, then food. That is the order of the house, and I did not make it. Where are you out of?
I know those feet. Sit. The brothers wrote down what you told us the last time, and I am to ask whether it was true.
It is a fast today. You are a guest, so it is not. The brothers are very glad to see you, for reasons of charity.
A stranger from over the sea is a grey dog in our law, with no price on his face. Under the abbot's word you are a man again. It is worth having.
Sailors from Gaul used to bring the wine and the year's news together. Now the wine comes seldom, and the news comes by itself.
Eat what is set before a guest
Say you will keep the fast with the house
Give a cask of wine for the Mass
Give them the year's news to write down
Mutton, on a fast day, with the whole house eating it for your sake and thanking God for sending you. You have never been so welcome anywhere for doing so little.

There is a silence, in which you can hear the brothers' hopes fall. Then the guest-master laughs until he has to sit down on the edge of the tub. A merchant, he says, holier than the rule. The abbot will want to look at you.

He tastes it from a horn spoon with his eyes shut. Nothing is priced here. He says what the house needs, and afterwards what the house gives: three bundles of sealskin, a name said at the altar, and a pair of feet that will be known at this tub from now on.

He asks three things at once and remembers all three answers. A boy cuts the heads of it on a stick: who is king where, what was burned, what a cow costs over the sea. It will go into a book, he says. You should have told it better.
Names for the altar

On a knoll of bare rock facing the church stands a small hut of planks with its door open to the Sound. A very old man sits in it, with a book satchel on a peg behind him. He asks what you know before he asks what you carry.

A hump of bare rock with a small plank hut on its top, the door open east over a wide sound of green water to pink rocks: inside, a very old, small monk with a crown tonsure and a plain crooked staff, a book satchel hung on a peg behind him, one hand held out toward the merchant; below, a timber church and tall stone crosses.
God's blessing on the boat and the men in her. You come from over the sea, so you have no standing here until I give it. I give it. Sit.
The same keel. Good. Columba said kings of strange peoples would honour this place. He did not mention merchants, but I do not think he would mind.
Our daughter house on the English shore was struck on the eve of our own saint's feast. If you have been there, tell me who is alive. I knew them by their letters.
You carry something folded in oiled skin, and you carry it as a man carries a thing he was told not to sell. Give it into my hand.
A cheese. From the kings' rock on the English shore. Then there is a message with it. There is always a message with a cheese.
They have come here now, as they came there. I look north before I look east. An old man should not have to learn a new habit.
Give the bishop's list into his own hand
Tell him what you saw on the English shore
Give him Muirenn's cheese, and her word
Ask what Columba foretold of the island

He reads it standing, which costs him something. On the next fast day the names are read at the altar with the whole house on its feet: the dead, the living, the boys. Afterwards he gives you his protection in writing, three lines of Latin, and a man of the outer islands is fetched who saw the ships go home that summer: north, rowing for the fjord country with their sails down.

The doors off the church, the cross head in the grass, the saint's coffin untouched. He wants names and you have few. He says them over after you, in Irish mouths that turn them strange, so as to have them for the altar.

The true Easter in her heart, and the Roman one in church. He laughs, a small dry sound like a leaf turning. He knew her brother: a tall man with bad teeth and a good voice. Tell her, he says, that the reckoning was settled before she was born, and that the blessing goes back with the rind.

Small and mean though this place is, he says, kings of the Irish and of strange peoples and their saints shall yet honour it. He stops there. There is more, about what comes after, and he tells that part to nobody under seventy.
The book of the four beasts

On the widest board in the writing house lies a calfskin leaf with one great letter on it and nothing else, full of beasts biting each other. At the next board a long stooped scribe breathes on his fingers, and looks at your bundle.

A long hut with the best light on the island: a row of sloped boards with calfskin leaves pinned on them, horns of ink, shells of colour, a goose wing; on the widest board a page bearing one huge letter crowded with interlaced beasts; beside it a long, stooped young scribe with a quill behind his ear and purple under his nails, breathing on his fingers.
Mind the door, the wind lifts the leaves. You carry skins? Calf, not sheep? Then you are the best thing to land here since Easter.
Ah, the merchant. The last skins were good. Two had fly-holes. I wrote round them, and nobody will notice for a thousand years.
The master does one great page in a season. I do the plain lines beside it. He is praised. I am legible.
The purple is a lichen off these rocks, and the blue is woad. People ask for the blue stone from beyond Rome. People may ask.
There is a verse in the margin of a grammar here, about a bitter wind. I did not write it. If you like it, I did.
The abbot packs books as other men pack fish. I have told the boatman how to stow a chest so often that he now does it wrong on purpose.
Hear him reckon the great book
Take the writing house's order stick
Ask for the verse about the wind
Look at the great letter, and touch nothing

The calves of a great herd, he says, the years of four scribes, and purple scraped off the island's own rocks. Then what a king's church would give for it, and what a heathen would give, for the cover alone. He says the second sum quietly, as a man names a sickness.

Cut on a stick by the guest-master's boy: calfskin without holes, woad, orpiment, red lead, copper green, oak gall. Not the blue stone. There is none in this book, and none wanted. The house gives a fifth over what such things fetch, in sealskin and in thanks.

He writes it out small, four lines, on an offcut too narrow for anything else. It is for a night of gale, he says, when no long ship can keep the sea. Your reader may say it aloud at anchor in bad weather. It works on monks. It may work on Frisians.

It tires the eye to follow one line of it: a beast's neck becomes a knot, and the knot a bird, and the bird's leg the stroke of the letter again. The scribe watches you try. Everybody tries, he says. The master says the trick is not to finish.
A chest for Kells

There are sixty-eight new graves in a row in Oran's ground. In the church the abbot shows you a chest of oak lined with waxed hide. In it, in loose gatherings, lies the great book, a third of its pages still bare.

A small dark timber church with one lamp and a stone altar: a strong, tonsured abbot of fifty with rolled sleeves lifting the lid of an oak chest lined with waxed hide, loose gatherings of a great painted book inside; the merchant looking in; two young monks standing by with nothing in their hands; through the door, a row of fresh graves.
Blessing on you. What is she, seven paces on the keel? Then she carries one chest and two brothers. Come up, and I will show you the chest.
People say I am leaving the island. I am moving the things that burn. The saint's grave does not burn, and neither do I.
To the black pool on the Liffey. Men of ours wait there with a cart. Keep the chest high, dry and aft of the mast. If she fills, save the brothers first. Do not tell them I said so.
I have never been in a boat with a keel. Does it lean? I was told that it leans.
Take the chest and the two brothers
Say the book is too dear for so small a boat, and carry timber
Say you are bound the other way

The chest goes under your own bench, lashed, on two billets clear of the bilge. The brothers sit one each side of it with their hands on the lid, and say the psalms through from the beginning as soon as the land is out of sight.

He does not argue. A man who knows what his boat will bear, he says, is rarer than a man who will try anything. Two loads of oak for the new roof, then, before next harvest, at half as much again as any yard would give.
He nods, gives you a blessing and an order to his monks in the same breath, and has already turned to the next thing. The chest will go in a hide boat, then, in whatever weather God sends.
Colum Cille's feast

It is the week of the saint's feast, and boats from every house of his family lie bottom up above the weed line. Before the church door, under the tall crosses, bargains are being sworn that would hold nowhere else. Here a stranger may bargain, for the saint stands surety.

Four great carved stone crosses before a timber church door on a bright early-summer day, pilgrims and monks crowding between them: a man of the islands with a bundle of otter skins laying his hand on a cross shaft, a broad bare-legged boatman standing witness, the merchant facing them with an open purse; hide boats bottom-up on white sand beyond.
Otter, taken on the Ross this winter. Ten to the bundle. I swear their number at the cross, you swear your silver, and the saint hears us both. It is cheaper than going to law.
On the feast I witness more bargains than I carry pilgrims. A man who breaks his word under that cross does not get a boat off this island from me.
I came from the Dee in a hide boat that has since gone home without me. I must be at Saint John's on the red cliff before harvest. I can pay a little, and pray rather more.
Swear a bargain for otter skins at the cross (30 d)
Carry the pilgrim home to the Dee
Keep the feast, and trade nothing

He lays his hand on the cross shaft and says the count. You lay yours beside it and say the weight. The boatman says he heard both. It is thirty pennies for a bundle worth forty anywhere with a king in it, and no court on earth would dare to hear it argued.

He pays twelve pennies, sewn into his hem one by one, and prays the whole of the first night aloud. By the second your men have him bailing. He knows the pilot of the Dee, he says: a sound man, and scornful, who once carried two monks of this house up the river and approved of them.

The psalms go on all night in voices that do not hurry, and in the morning every boat on the sand is blessed in turn, yours among them, by a brother with a branch and a bucket. Your men are wet, and pleased, and say it was well worth the salt.
The frozen sea

On the western plain a brother stands apart from the reapers, watching the sky over the sea, because a crane is expected from Ireland and the house has orders about cranes. He has the look of a man who has seen further in that direction than he is saying.

A flat green plain of shell-sand turf with barley in strips and black cattle, white beaches and open ocean beyond: monks reaping in a line with their habits hitched up, and one brother standing apart with his hand shading his eyes, looking west into an empty sky; the merchant beside him; high bright cloud.
I was half a year on an island in the north with two brothers. At midsummer the sun only hid behind a little hill, and a man could pick the lice from his shirt at midnight as well as at noon.
A day's sail north of that, the sea itself is frozen. Before you reach it, things come along the wave: white, sharp-edged, laughing horribly against the hull. I have a verse on them.
We do not go now. There are robbers from the north on those islands, and nothing left there but sheep and sea-birds. It is a pity. It was very quiet.
One of us has written it down, in a book on the measure of the earth. He asked me the distances. I gave him days. He wanted more.
Hear his verse of the thing that came along the wave
Ask for a copy of what was written down
Watch for the crane with him

A thing came sailing along the wave, he says, comely and strange; it called to the land, and its laughter was terrible; its edges were sharp. And it said of itself that its mother was also its daughter. He will not say what it is. He has seen one. He says that is not the same as knowing.

A leaf in a small quick hand: the island where the sun hides behind a hill, the frozen sea a day beyond it, and the little islands two days and nights from the north of Britain, full of sheep and empty of hermits. We have not seen these islands named in any author, the writer says. The brother seems rather proud of that.

It comes at evening, low and worn out, and falls on the sand like a dropped cloak. He carries it up to the guest house in his arms. Three days' care, he says, and then it flies home to Ireland. The saint ordered it so for the first one, and nobody has countermanded him.
The seals' islet

Off the island's end a skerry of wet black rock is covered with seals, and the noise is like a hall at a feast heard through a wall. A short, wide man in a sealskin cap is bailing a hide boat, and has plainly been expecting you to hold too far west.

A skerry of wet black rock crowded with grey and spotted seals and white pups, skins drying on a frame, a stone trough for oil: in front, on white sand, a short, wide-shouldered boatman in a salt-white wool shirt and sealskin cap bailing a hide boat with a wooden bailer, looking up at the merchant; green water over shell sand.
You came in past the Torran rocks with nobody aboard who knows them? Then the saint likes you. Next time take me.
I saw the sail off Erraid and said: that is the Frisian, and he still holds too far west. Welcome back.
They are the house's own herd, taken by count, as a farmer takes lambs. A man of Colonsay once hid under his boat to steal them. The saint sent him home with sheep. We still count.
They burned the house. I tow oak over from the lochs behind the boat, a tree at a time. A second keel would halve it.
The guest-master says you are a known pair of feet. Then you have skins at the house's reckoning, which is less than I would ask of a stranger.
Give two sacks of salt for sealskins
Tow timber with him for the burned house
Hire him past the Torran rocks (2 d)
Count the seals with him

He rubs the salt between finger and thumb, and has two bundles of skins off the frame before you have named anything. The house wants salt for the curing more than it wants silver, of which it has no notion.

Two days of it, with an oak trunk wallowing astern like a drowned ox. When the last one grounds on the white sand he says nothing, and takes you out in his own boat, and shows you the marks through the Sound and round the Torran rocks at every state of the tide. Then a place on the west side where a keel can lie hidden under hay.

He is unhurried and exact about water, and vague about everything else. He gives the rocks more room than seems manly, and says so before you can. The Sound has drowned men who knew it, he says. Do not know it too well.

A hundred and four, and eleven pups since the last count. He can tell you the weather for three days, which skerries have a landing, and who is shouting from Mull by the shout. Kings, he says, shout once.
Under the turf

Word has come from Tiree of long ships working south. The shrine of Colum Cille is on the island this summer. A king's son who chose this house because it was dangerous has had it buried under turf, and after the night office he speaks to the brothers. Then he turns to you.

First grey light on white sand below a turf bank: a tall, calm monk of forty standing before a half circle of frightened brothers who hold nothing in their hands; a broad old boatman pointing north with his bailer; the merchant by his boat, her bow already afloat; behind the bank, a square of freshly laid turf beside a timber church.
Those who can bear what is coming may stay with me. Those who cannot should go by the path they know, and not be ashamed. I asked for this place. They did not.
Merchant. How many will your boat hold?
A long ship rounds the Ross in half a morning with this wind. The house has until tomorrow. I can hide a keel on the west side under hay, for a man who wants to say afterwards that he saw.
I have nothing in my hands. He ordered it. I should like you to see that I am taking nothing.
Take the brothers who choose to go, to Ireland
Hide the boat on the west side, and watch
Put to sea now, and take nobody

Nine of them, wading out with their habits round their waists and nothing in their hands. Nobody looks back, which takes all nine of them a great effort. Three days to the Liffey. The house never forgets which keel it was: lodging and stores at cost for you and yours for as long as there are brothers on the island.

They come at first light. He meets them at the church door. You are too far off to hear what is said, and are told later by one who was nearer: that he did not know where the gold lay, and would not say if he did. What you see, you see. Your men do not speak of it for a season, and they look at you a little differently.

You are round the south end before the tide turns, with an empty boat and a fair wind. Nothing is lost by it but warmth. When you next lie on the white sand, the brothers who came back are civil, and count what you bring twice.
Whose skull is the sky

A Northman is on his knees at a cross slab in Oran's ground, cutting the grass back from the runes with a knife. He will not riddle on holy ground. He looks at the sand below the bank, and then at the sun, which has an hour left.

A walled plot of small crosses and flat slabs cropped by sheep, late sun: a fair-haired Northman in a blue cloak with a silver ring brooch kneeling at a slab carved with a cross and a line of runes, trimming the grass from it with a knife; a small cross and a small hammer on one thong at his neck; the merchant standing at the wall; white sand and green water below.
You lie beside me on the sand, so we share the watch. I come here for one who is under that stone. I had the runes cut myself. The monks' letters would be strange to him.
The merchant with the long memory. What does the penny weigh at Chester this year? The Dublin one is honest for the moment. I say for the moment.
They tell old questions in the halls of Dublin and York, in a row, like men passing a horn. The last of the row is kept here. I do not give it to a man who has not drunk from the others.
You have answered York's. I see it on you. Come down to the sand at evening. Not here. He was baptised, and I will not ask a giant's question over him.
A boat. Yes. The oldest thing the old giant could remember was a boat. Now lay the answers side by side, as you would lay strakes, and see what shore they make.
Go down to the sand at evening for the last question
Tell him you have all the answers, and ask what shore they make
Help him clear the grass from the stone

On the white sand, with his back to the crosses, he asks it: what is the furthest thing back that you bear in mind, wise giant? He says it in his own tongue first, and then again for you, and crosses himself afterwards, a little ashamed of both halves.

From the flood, by a boat, to a south bank, he says slowly. There is a river in the English land, a day north of the Dee, where the people driven out of Dublin came ashore and an army put its chest in the ground. Ask a Dee pilot for the Ribble. Say that a man tending a grave sent you.

You hold the turf back while he cuts. The runes say who laid the stone, and over whom, and nothing else. My father's father came to these islands to take things, he says. I come to lay a stone. The sea is the same. We got older.
The old king's pennies

The abbot meets the boat on the white sand. The old king walks up to the church without looking back at the sea. Afterwards, in the guest house, a bag of some hundreds of English pennies is held out to you as a man holds a live eel.

White shell sand under a turf bank: an abbot with a small bronze bell at his belt standing before the merchant's beached boat; a big-framed, gaunt old man in a penitent's coarse grey tunic, the pale mark of arm-rings on his wrists, walking away up the path toward tall crosses without looking back; a monk holding a heavy bag at arm's length.
He is received as a penitent, and will be buried as one. This house has never struck a coin or counted one. Weigh this for us, merchant, and say what it is in ounces, and in cows.
I had a hall once with a door wide enough for six men abreast. Here I duck my head. It is a better door. Tell Sitriuc his father sleeps on straw and sleeps well. He will not believe either part.
You carried me for a ring and asked nothing more. I have been carried by many men. Most of them wanted a kingdom for it.
Weigh the bag truly, and say it in cows
Weigh it a little light, and keep the difference

Three hundred and fifty pennies: near enough thirty ounces, thirty good cows, or the food of this house for a winter. The abbot has the bag put in the church, unspent, since there is nothing on the island to spend it on. When the king's son hears who carried his father, no toll is taken from your house at the long stone while he lives.

Nobody on the island can check a scale. The old king can. He watches your hand from his straw and says nothing, and smiles, as a man smiles who has done the same thing to better men. Forty pennies. They are heavier in the purse than they weighed.
A grey dog

A round house of woven hazel stands just inside the gap in the bank, its door never barred. A spare old man with a bundle of tally sticks watches you come up from the pool, and points at a tub of water before he says a word.

A round house of woven hazel just inside the gap of a wide earth bank, its door open and a fire inside: goods laid out on a hide before the door, three men standing by as sureties; a spare, upright old man in a brown cloak with a bronze ring-pin and a bundle of notched sticks pointing the merchant to a tub of water; a wooden church with a shingled roof behind.
A boat from over the sea, and no host. Sit, wash your feet. Until I say you are my guest you are a grey dog here, and anyone may kick you.
My guest again. Good. The sureties are the same three men, and one of them has been asking after your wine since the cattle went up.
Not hard to tell. A cask of wine is a milch cow and her calf. Salt before the slaughter is worth more than salt after. Nothing here is worth silver, since nobody has any.
There has been no abbot since Siadal. The kin argue over whose son it should be. Meanwhile I count the calves, and God, I hope, counts me.
The fishermen saw smoke off Rechru for three days. They say the ships had no oars showing and went like gulls. I have buried the altar cup.
Give him a cask of wine, and first choice of the cargo
Give salt, and trade through his sureties this once
Ask what things are worth here, in cows
Stay a grey dog, and trade with nobody

He tastes the wine, names three men, and says before them that you are his guest. From that word you have a price on your face in this country: a wrong done to you can be sued for. Two bundles of hides come down to the boat, since a gift here looks hard for its return.

A sack of salt on the hide before his door. He calls the three men, the bargain is said aloud, and for this visit what you sell is sold safely. A bargain said to the wind, he tells you, is the wind's.

He tells it slowly and exactly: a milch cow, a heifer, a sack of malt, an ounce of silver if any were ever seen. Wine and salt and iron on one side, hides and cloaks and hounds on the other. He names the sureties before he names the goods.
You fill your water casks at the pool and nobody stops you. Nobody sells you anything either. A boy throws a clod at your steersman, to see whether it is true that he may, and it is.
The chest on the strand

The ferryman brings you over the bar himself, and will take no fee from Columba's people. At the pool, men of Kells are waiting with a cart and eight spears. Before anybody is paid, a brother kneels in the mud and opens the chest.

The muddy lip of a dark pool with boats stern to the reeds: an oak chest open on the strand, a young monk kneeling over loose painted gatherings with his sleeves pushed back; behind him an ox cart and eight spearmen; a lean grey-tonsured monk with a wax tablet looking on; across the water, a single cloaked rider waiting.
Dry. Every gathering. I have counted them twice with my thumb. I did not think it could be done in a boat that leans.
I am told what is in it. I should like to see it, once. I ask politely. I shall not ask again. It is a rule of mine.
My lord across the river has a sick child. He would give ten cows for one painted leaf, to lay on the boy. One leaf of so many. Nobody need know. I shall wait at the ford until dark.
Hand the chest over whole, and see it onto the cart
Let the monk of Tallaght look inside first
Let the king of Brega's man have one painted leaf, at dusk

The lid goes down and the cart goes north-west with eight spears round it. You are paid as abbeys pay: wax, fine cloaks, a letter, and a protector at every house of Columba's family from here to the English shore. Word of it reaches the island before your boat does.

The brother with the key looks at you, and you nod. The monk lifts one gathering with the tips of his fingers: a page with a great letter on it, and beasts biting each other. He looks for as long as a psalm takes. Then he says a blessing on the scribes, and on the boat, and counts something on his fingers.

Ten cows' worth, in weighed silver, since you cannot carry cows. One leaf of so many. The brothers count the gatherings again at the cart, as you knew they would, and their thumbs stop. No house of Columba's family will give you so much as a letter to carry in your lifetime, and they will say why.
A day with no saint in it

A morning's walk toward the hills there is a tight bank, a small church, and cells in rows, everything swept. In the writing hut a lean monk rules lines on calfskin by the light of the door, and counts something on his fingers when he sees you.

A tightly banked monastery under hills, cells in swept rows, monks standing knee-deep in a stream saying psalms: in the door of a writing hut a lean monk of forty-five with a grey-edged tonsure, ink on two fingers and a wax tablet at his belt, ruling lines on a calfskin and glancing up at the merchant, who is standing in his light.
A merchant. Good. Tell me what saint your church at home keeps, and on what day. No, I want nothing else. Sit. You are standing in my light.
You again, and I have filled eleven days since. Have you a name for me from over the water, or only casks?
My master said the ale that makes men forget God would not be drunk here. So we remember God, and are thirsty.
I have a day in harvest with no saint in it. If a holy man died among the Frisians about then, I should count it a kindness.
Your bishop of the Maas has his line in the harvest quarter now, between two Irishmen. He will find them good company. They talk less than he does.
Give him the days your own churches keep
