Give him a bundle of calfskin for the calendar
Ask him to read a leaf out of your chest
Sit out of his light and watch him rule

Willibrord, four days before Martinmas. Martin himself. Boniface, in the week before your own Colum Cille. And for the harvest, a bishop killed on the Maas twelve days before Michaelmas: Lambert. He writes each on his tablet, and looks at the last one as a farmer looks at a full barn.

He turns each skin to the light, finds no fly-holes, and for once has nothing dry to say. He will read and write Latin letters for your house without fee from this day, he says at last, and the brothers will say your name. It is all a client of God has to pay with.

He reads it aloud without smiling, which costs him something, and then again with his finger under each word so that you can follow. He corrects one letter with a wet thumb. Whoever wrote that, he says, was cold.

He pricks the margin with an awl, lays a straight edge, and draws a blind line with a bone point: thirty to the leaf, and not one crooked. A saint to every line, he says, for every day of the year. He has three hundred and some. He does not say how many some.
The hurdles and the bar

Woven hurdles show at low water as a pale crooked line from bank to bank, and four roads come down to them out of the hills. A short wide man with a sounding pole worn pale by his hands has been waiting on the bank since he saw your sail off the head.

A wide brown river at low water with a pale crooked line of woven hurdles pegged across its bed, cattle being driven over with shouting, a punt and a hide boat drawn up by a round wattle house: in front a short, wide, bare-legged ferryman with black hair tied back and a long pale sounding pole, pointing seaward for the merchant.
I saw you off the head at first light. You came in a spear's length from the bar and never knew. Next time wave, and I will come out.
The same boat, a little lower in the water. Trade is good, then. The bar has moved a ship's length south since you left. Follow me in.
You paid for the hurdles. The ford remembers, and so do I. The bar is two boat-lengths off the black post this spring. I say it before you ask.
Forty head crossed yesterday going north, and no herdsman I knew. Somebody is paying a fine, or stealing one.
They took women off Benn Étair, a whole strand of them. My wife will not go down for weed now unless I stand on the rock.
Follow him over the bar, and pay him in bread (2 d)
Pay for new hurdles at the ford (90 d)
Ask who has crossed this month
He goes ahead in the punt, sounding as he poles, and calls the depths back in tides and spear-lengths. The river tells you its depth twice a day, he says. A man who drowns here was not listening.

Hazel is cut, woven and pegged across the river bed at the next low water, and four roads' worth of drovers bless your name without knowing it. He shows you his own marks for the bar: the black post, the thorn on the ridge, the smoke of the church. His kin, he says, will tell them back to yours for as long as there is a ford.

He has a tally in his head of every boat that has lain in the pool in his time, and every herd that has crossed. A king's steward going north with a fine. Three monks in a hide boat with no steering oar: he asked where to, and they said God knew. He hopes that God told them.
The ship-fort

A raw turf bank with a fence of split oak on top stands open to the river, and inside it long hulls are drawn up on rollers with their masts down. A man who has plainly not kept a harbour for long weighs your boat with his eye, and holds out his hand.

A raw turf bank topped with a split-oak fence, open to a tidal river: inside it a row of long low hulls on rollers with their masts down, tents and booths of sailcloth between them, armed men mending gear; a heavy Northman with a plaited beard holding out an open hand to the merchant's boat; a man carving a small board on an upturned cask; tar smoke.
You lie under our bank, so you pay our share. That is the whole law here. It is short, and everybody understands it.
We have silver, hides and people. We have no bread. It is always grain. Bring rye before the winter, and name your weight.
A board with pegs, so the pieces stay put in a seaway. And a question that goes with it for nothing, if you buy: what beast is girdled with iron, has eight horns, and no head?
There is a king in the fort now, a son of the king of Lochlann, and the Irish pay him. Before him we paid ourselves. It came to much the same.
Pay the fort's share, and trade
Sell them wheat, for silver by weight
Take the fort's order for rye before winter
Buy a pegged board from the carver (6 d)

He takes his share by weight on a folding scale and bites nothing, which you take as a courtesy. After that nobody in the fort looks at your boat twice. It is the safest mooring you have ever disliked.

Twelve pennies' weight the sack, in cut arm rings and coin from four kingdoms, and the wheat is carried off before the scale has stopped swinging. They do not thank you. They ask when you are coming back, which here is the same thing.

Eight sacks before the cattle come down from the hills, he says, at half as much again as any Frank would pay, and no share taken on that load. He does not cut a tally. He looks at your face for a while instead, which he says keeps longer.

It is a neat thing of yew, seven holes by seven, with a ring cut round the middle one. He says the question over again as he hands you the pegs, and grins. He had it from his father, who never told him the answer either.
The strand of the captives

On the hard sand below the bank people sit roped by the ankle in rows, sorted by tongue, with a folding scale laid on a sea chest. Nobody shouts. The dealer looks at your keel before he looks at you, and seems to find it honest.

A stretch of hard sand below a turf bank: rows of people sitting roped by the ankle, sorted into groups, hides stacked as high as a man behind them; a heavy, fair-bearded dealer in a blue cloak with a silver ring-pin and a folding bronze scale on a sea chest, looking at the merchant's boat; in the nearest row a young man half risen, calling out; flat grey light.
A Frisian keel. You have a scale, I hope. Mine is true, but you should not have to take a stranger's word for his own weights.
You came back. Most do not, after the first look at my strand. Sit. I have grain to buy before I have anything to sell.
The kings are home from the rock on the Clyde. Two hundred ships. The price is not the best. I mean that it has halved.
You! Frisian! I know the cut of that sail. I have seen it in the Tyne. I am Osgar, a reeve's son from north of that river. My kin would pay. I can tally. I can read.
I heard. You carried one home and asked only his cost. A buyer like that is offered the next lot first, at the first weight I name.
If you buy from me, do not sell south to the Franks. They ask where a Christian came from.
Buy the young Englishman, to carry him home (30 d)
Sell him wheat first, as he asks
Weigh one penny on his scale and on yours
Walk on down the strand

Thirty pennies' weight and no haggling, the dealer says, and means it. The rope comes off with one cut. The young man stands in your bow the whole way out of the bay and does not once look at the strand. He asks only whether you go north about, or by the Dee and over the hills.

He weighs your wheat on your scale and his silver on his own, and the two agree to a grain. A bad winter in the fort with too many mouths roped on his strand, he says, is the one thing he fears. He calls that not the best kind of winter.

The same, to the breadth of a hair. He nods, and tells you who on this strand has a light scale, and what a captive of each people fetches here, at York and in the east. He says it as a man tells the price of wool. Among his people it is the price of wool.
You walk the length of it with your eyes on the water. Your men are quiet at their oars that evening. One of them, who was a boy when the long ships came to his own shore, does not eat.
The eldest of that kin

In the king's hall men speak Norse at one end and Irish at the other. By the king's seat stands a tall stooped poet with one silver arm ring and a rune-cut stick behind his belt. He has decided that you have a face which has been asked things.

A long wattle hall with four great roof posts and a fire down the middle, shields on the wall and silk on the high bench: beside the king's seat a tall, stooped poet with thinning red-brown hair, a green tunic with a silk band at the neck and a rune-cut stick behind his belt, beckoning the merchant to a place below the fire; wet dogs; meat smoke.
A merchant in the king's hall. Sit below the fire. Do you buy words, or only hides?
The man who answers. I have kept a seat and a question. The second is easier to keep than the first, in this hall.
The first is ten pennies' weight: of what was the earth made, and the sky? York's poet sells the same, and says it worse.
You have the first. Then say it to my face, not to York's, and I will give you the one that grows out of it.
The men who taught me sat on a bench with men who knew an old Northman called Ravn, who went to sea with Frisians and set them riddles. The questions came down from such men.
You know the river now. I see it. I was nine when my father carried a chest out of the old fort, and then one day he was not carrying it. What will you do at the end?
We left ships half built on the strand when the Irish came over the bank. I think about those ships.
Buy the first question (10 d)
Say the first answer to his face
Tell him where the silver lies, and dig with the heirs of 902
Sit below the fire and listen

He takes the silver by weight and gives the question measured out like verse: in the earliest time, whence came the earth, and the sky? The earth, he says, is under your feet. So do not complain to him afterwards that the answer was far to seek.

A giant's flesh, his bones, his skull, his blood. He hears it out and gives the next without being paid: which giant was first fashioned, and eldest of that kin? Then, more quietly, he tells you whose bench these questions came down from, and asks whether the name Ravn means anything in a Frisian house.

You tell him the river and the bank. He is silent for the length of a verse. It was his fathers' silver, and he had thought it would be a stranger who dug it. Men of the old families go with you. Yours is a finder's part, and a plot on the plank street free of the king's share, and his word for you in this hall and in York's.

He praises the king in a verse so knotted that the Irish end of the hall takes it for an insult and the Norse end for a compliment. Both are partly right. He catches your eye as he finishes, and lifts one shoulder.
The long stone

A tall grey standing stone marks the strand east of the town. Below it hulls lie side by side on a bank of clay and wattle, and porters carry casks up a plank path to a gate. The king's man sits on an upturned boat with a scale on his knee.

A tall grey standing stone on a strand, hulls lying side by side along a bank of clay and wattle, porters with casks on a plank path up to a gate in an earth bank, smoke of many hearths beyond: on an upturned boat a man in a fur-edged cloak with a small scale, looking over the merchant's bales; a striped sail furled behind.
The king's share is taken on what you land, by weight. I weigh once. If you think my scale light, bring your own, and we shall argue like friends.
The house that carried the old king. I am to take nothing from you while his son lives. I weigh it anyway, for the pleasure of giving it back.
Black stone from the English cliff, tried by the straw? The ring-cutters on the plank street give half as much again for that as York does. I only tell you because I want a ring.
Under the Irish king nothing is loaded, sold or carried from Saturday's evening to Monday's morning. An ounce of silver from the man who forgets, and his load besides.
Every plot in the town owes the king of Tara an ounce of gold each Christmas night. Gold. In a town of silver-weighers. If you have any, you have friends.
Weigh out the king's share
Remind him whose house you are
Sell tested jet to the ring-cutters
Buy a timber of marten skins at Dublin's price (80 d)
He weighs once, as he said, and the scale is true. The share goes into a chest with three locks. Go in the king's peace as far as it reaches, he says, which is the bar. After that, be quick.
He puts the scale away unopened. A king all his life, he says, and went out like a pilgrim with one bag, in your people's boat. They tell it in the alehouse in both tongues. Lie where you like.

On the plank street a man tries your stone with a straw, then with a hot needle, and then stops trying. Fifty-four pennies' weight the sack, in arm-ring ends and a few thin coins. They want it for rings and gaming pieces. He gives the king's man a ring. You notice that.

Forty skins on a cord, dark and glossy, for two thirds of what they fetch on the English side. The seller asks nothing about where they are going. The reeve at the Dee will ask, and will want to see them first.
The old king's passage

After the battle at Tara the town is full of men settling debts. An old man with the marks of rings on his wrists, and two silent servants behind him, asks the price of a passage to Colum Cille's island. He pays it without haggling, for the first time in his life.

The strand below the long stone on a grey day, a town of thatched plots behind an earth bank with its gate standing open: a big-framed, gaunt old man in a plain grey cloak, white beard cut short, pale ring marks on his bare wrists, one bag at his feet and two silent servants behind, looking at the merchant's small boat; one mended sandal.
I was king here forty years, and in York twice. My sons lost in a day at Tara what took me all of that. I am going to the monks. Do not look so. It was that or drink.
The king of Tara stood at my gate, and every Irish slave in the town walked out past him free. I counted them. Old habit.
One bag. A king all my life, and it comes down to one bag and a boat with four oars. Is she dry?
Carry him for the ring he offers
Carry him, and take nothing
Say your boat is bound for the Dee

A ring-pin of gold, heavy as a small bird, paid in advance as a king pays who has been cheated by experts. He sits amidships on his bag with his back to the town. Past the bar he asks what a slave fetches on this strand now, and then asks you to tell him to repent of asking.

He looks at you for some time, to see what you want instead. When he finds that it is nothing, he laughs, the only time on the passage. He has been carried by many men, he says. He had forgotten it could be done for no reason.

He nods as a man nods who has been refused very seldom and is trying to learn how it is taken. He finds another boat by evening. The king's man at the landing weighs your goods twice that day, and finds them light both times.
The law mound

South of the river stands a steep green mound with a ring of posts on its flat top. On a law day the free men of the town stand round its foot. Today a Dublin skipper stands on its side and says your boat's name aloud, twice, so that none can claim not to have heard.

A steep green mound as high as six men with a ring of posts on its flat top, outside a town bank: free men standing round its foot, an old man with a staff half way up its side, and beside him a Dublin skipper pointing down at the Frisian merchant, who stands at the foot with two townsmen at his elbows; gulls; wind in cloaks.
His keel lay across my stern line on the ebb and parted it. I lost an anchor and a tide. I say it twice, as the law wants: an anchor and a tide.
A stranger may answer here if he has two sworn men of the town beside him. Without them he may pay, or he may go, and not come back.
And the Irish king has laid his own rule on this strand: no bale opened and no keel loaded while the Lord rests. We did not ask for it. We keep it.
Answer him on the mound, with two sworn men
Pay him the worth of his anchor (12 d)
Offer him your spare anchor stone and a day's work

Two men from the alehouse stand beside you and swear to where your boat lay, and your steersman shows the mark of the other man's line on your own stem. The lawman says it twice: no claim. The skipper shrugs, and offers to drink on it. It was worth trying, he says.

Your two sworn men agree with each other about everything but the tide. The lawman says it twice: an anchor's worth, and a fine to the king for the mound's time. The skipper is gracious about it, having expected less.

Twelve pennies' weight, said aloud and weighed at the foot of the mound. The free men go home disappointed. The skipper tells you where to buy a better anchor than the one he lost, which you suspect was never much of an anchor.

Your men grumble and do it: a new stone slung in his old crook, his line spliced, his boat hauled a length up the strand. By evening he is telling the alehouse that Frisians are slow to pay silver and quick to pay sweat, and that he prefers it.
The alehouse by the ford road

Just inside the west gate, where the road from the ford comes in, a wattle house larger than its neighbours has a bush tied over the door. Inside are one hearth, two benches, a vat, and a woman with keys at her belt who is already telling you to shut the door.

A wattle house with a bush tied over the door, inside: one hearth, two benches, a vat, a board for dice, men of three tongues drinking; a broad, quick, dark-haired woman in a red-brown gown pinned with one old oval brooch, keys and a small knife at her belt, pointing the merchant to a bench with a dipper; smoke and boiled mutton.
Shut the door, you are letting the smoke out. Frisian? My people have a story about a Frisian boat. Sit down, and I will see if it is you.
There he is. You owe me for two cups from the last time, and I owe you a story. We will call it even if you bring salt.
A boat a spear's length from the bar, a ferryman who waved, and a Frisian who paid for the hurdles. That is the story. Six or seven lives back. You have the same nose.
The king of Tara stood at the gate, and every Irish slave in the town walked out past him. I lost a cook. I did not mind as much as I said.
An ounce of gold on every plot, each Christmas night. I asked the steward if he took ale instead. He did not laugh. He drank it, though.
Hire the hand she names (8 d)
Tell her it was your house that paid for the hurdles
Drink, and settle the old cups (2 d)
Sit, and listen to who is hiring for which ship

A lad with a Norse father and an Irish mother, like half the town, who has rowed to Man and back and can swear at a toll man in either tongue. She tells you his one fault, which is dice, and the name of the man he owes.

She stops with the dipper in the air. Then she tells it to the whole house, in both tongues, with the ferryman's wave and the bar a spear's length off, and you are made to stand up. The marks for the bar are the same as they were, she says, less the thorn tree, which a king burned.
She remembers what you drank and what you owed, to the half cup. Three things a house cannot hide, she says, taking the pennies: smoke, a full vat, and a man who owes.

Who is in the town, who has left, which king is over it this year and what he wants at Christmas. She tells it across three other talks without losing the thread of any. Mind the bar going out, she adds. It has moved. Her people always say that.
Sixty oars
A long keel lies on blocks above the tide line with half her strakes on, pale oak against the mud. A thick-armed man with a broad axe has left her to walk round your boat, knocking on her as he goes.

A strand above the tide line: a very long keel on blocks with half her strakes fitted, pale new oak against dark mud, men splitting a log with wedges, steam rising from a plank bent over a fire; in front a thick-armed wright with chips in his grey-fair beard and a broad axe on his shoulder, knuckles raised to knock on the merchant's small old boat.
That boat. Danish-built, small, old in her lines. Who keeps a thing like that sailing? Bring her up on the rollers and let me look underneath.
She is still afloat, then. I told the boy she would be. I have a strake of dry oak put by with your house's mark on it.
I have a keel laid thirty paces long. Sixty oars. The king who ordered her may not be the king who launches her. She will not care.
The oak comes dearer each year. Somebody burned a wood to spite somebody's god. A wood does not grow back for a grandson.
A wright on the Ouse sends me iron, and I send him seasoned knees. Neither of us has seen the other's face. I should know his adze work anywhere.
Take his order for rivets
Have her hauled, and let him look underneath (20 d)
Watch them bend a strake
Ten thousand rivets go into a long ship, he says, and he has iron for six. Six kegs before the next launching season, and he pays well over what any smith would ask, in silver of the right weight.

He spends a tide under her with a lamp and comes out saying only that she will do. From him that is a song of praise. He scarfs a new length into her third strake from the dry oak he had put by, and cuts your house's mark where only the next wright will find it.

A plank as long as your boat goes over the fire, is wetted, and bends to the stem like a bow being strung. One man counts. A ship, the wright says, is a hundred small things that must all be done. A king is one large thing that need not be.
King Æthelred of the Northumbrians is killed by his own men at Corbridge, a week before the Litany. Osbald is made king in his place.
